順天府鄉試錄序

聖天子臨御二十八載，秋八月，賓興屆期，順天府臣以考試官請。上命臣大和、臣樸輟館事，主其事。臣大和聞命驚惕，竊伏自念：海濱賤士，叨蒙皇上作養詞林十有五年，雖嘗分校禮闈、編摩史局，日鰓鰓焉，無以報塞為懼。乃今膺茲簡命，敢不矢公矢明，惟寅惟慎，以求稱任使邪？越甲辰，陛辭入院，則府尹臣奎、府丞臣一桂先事經畫，百需咸備。御史臣
translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination

In the autumn, in the eighth month of the twenty-eighth year of the sagely Son of Heaven’s reign, the appointed time arrived for honoring and advancing worthy candidates. The officials of Shuntian Prefecture requested the appointment of Examiners. His Majesty commanded us, his servants Dahe and Pu, to suspend our duties at the Hanlin Academy and take charge of the examination. On receiving this command, I, Dahe, was startled and apprehensive. I humbly reflected: a lowly scholar from the seacoast, I have undeservedly enjoyed His Majesty’s cultivation in the Hanlin Academy for fifteen years. Although I have previously served as an Associate Examiner in the Metropolitan Examination and compiled historical works in the Historiography Office, I have worried daily, fearing that I had no means of repaying his favor. Now that I have received this appointment, how could I fail to pledge impartiality and discernment, and act with reverence and caution, seeking to prove worthy of the responsibility entrusted to me?

On the jiachen day, we took leave of His Majesty and entered the examination compound. The Prefect, your servant Kui, and the Vice Prefect, your servant Yigui, had planned matters in advance, and every requirement was fully provided for. The Censor, your servant …

…Zhen and your servant Yicheng bore responsibility for supervising the examination. Those who divided the Classics among themselves for reviewing the papers were your servant Shi, a metropolitan graduate (jinshi); your servant Yingyuan, a Prefectural Judge; your servants Wenwei and Shan, Magistrates; and your servants Chaoyong, Ao, Zuo, [name transcribed as 𤐣; reading uncertain], and Bin, Instructors. All were outstanding men of the examination ranks who came in response to invitations. That evening, the Southern Pole Star shone brilliantly, and the stellar lodge Kui gleamed with color. All said: “These are signs of ten thousand years of imperial longevity and manifestations of cultural brilliance.” Thereupon they congratulated and admonished one another.

title: 嘉靖二十八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
明以来人文始日趨於盛蓋自胡
元僭據三光五岳之氣鬱而不
宣而人才因以壅閼我
太祖高皇帝用夏變夷首崇文教以
兵興之後經籍殘缺迺於洪武
辛酉頒五經四書于北方學校
又選國子生分教北方士始喁
===
喁然知嚮學矣人文其基於此
乎我
成祖文皇帝定鼎燕都闡揚儒術於
永樂乙未舉會試于
京師喜京闈初開首得畿士遂以
布衣
召見錫賚優渥士益蒸蒸焉感奮

乎我
成祖文皇帝定鼎燕都闡揚儒術於
永樂乙未舉會試于
京師喜京闈初開首得畿士遂以

召見錫賚優渥士益蒸蒸焉感奮
punctuated:
明以来，人文始日趨於盛。蓋自胡元僭據，三光五岳之氣鬱而不宣，而人才因以壅閼。我太祖高皇帝用夏變夷，首崇文教。以兵興之後，經籍殘缺，迺於洪武辛酉頒五經四書于北方學校，又選國子生分教北方，士始喁喁然知嚮學矣。人文其基於此乎？
我成祖文皇帝定鼎燕都，闡揚儒術。於永樂乙未，舉會試于京師，喜京闈初開首得畿士，遂以布衣召見，錫賚優渥，士益蒸蒸焉感奮。
translation_en:
…Since the advent of our Ming dynasty, literary culture has begun to flourish more with each passing day. During the usurpation of the non-Chinese Yuan, the vital energies of the Three Luminaries and Five Sacred Peaks were pent up and unable to circulate, and human talent was consequently obstructed. Our Emperor Taizu Gao transformed the non-Chinese through the ways of Chinese civilization, giving foremost importance to literary education. Because the classical texts were incomplete after the outbreak of warfare, in the xinyou year of Hongwu (1381) he distributed the Five Classics and Four Books to schools in the north. He also selected students of the Directorate of Education to teach throughout the north. Only then did scholars begin eagerly to turn toward learning. Was this not the foundation of literary culture here?
Our Emperor Chengzu Wen established his capital at Yandu and promoted Confucian learning. In the yiwei year of Yongle (1415), he held the Metropolitan Examination in the capital. Delighted that the first examination held there had yielded a scholar from the capital region, he summoned him to an audience while he was still a commoner and bestowed generous gifts upon him. Scholars were increasingly stirred and inspired…

title: 嘉靖二十八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
茲人文之初盛乎
列聖相承益隆無替逮我
皇上中興
至仁達孝倫制兼盡而
文謨之昭
敷言之訓方行天下至于海表罔
不翕然化成矧
===
京師首善之地濡染尤先蓋自壬
午紀元逮茲己酉凡十舉賢科
而譽髦之士日斌斌相望茲人
文之極盛也今觀其入試之文
雖言人人殊類能闡發理原苞
并今古有氣抱關洛者有秀兼
江浙者有雄軼湖蜀者有制備

京師首善之地濡染尤先蓋自壬
午紀元逮茲己酉凡十舉賢科
而譽髦之士日斌斌相望茲人
文之極盛也今觀其入試之文
雖言人人殊類能闡發理原苞
幷今古有氣抱關洛者有秀兼
江浙者有雄軼湖蜀者有制備
punctuated: 茲人文之初盛乎？列聖相承，益隆無替。逮我皇上中興，至仁達孝，倫制兼盡，而文謨之昭、敷言之訓，方行天下，至于海表，罔不翕然化成。矧京師首善之地，濡染尤先。蓋自壬午紀元，逮茲己酉，凡十舉賢科，而譽髦之士日斌斌相望，茲人文之極盛也。今觀其入試之文，雖言人人殊，類能闡發理原，苞并今古。有氣抱關洛者，有秀兼江浙者，有雄軼湖蜀者，有制備
translation_en: …Was this the first flowering of literary culture here? Successive sage emperors carried it forward, bringing ever greater prosperity without decline. With the restoration under our present Emperor, supreme benevolence and consummate filial piety have fully realized both human relationships and institutional order. His illustrious cultural counsels and the instruction proclaimed in his words now spread throughout the realm, reaching even beyond the seas; all alike are transformed by them. How much more so in the capital, the foremost seat of moral excellence, which receives their influence before all other places. From the renwu year marking the beginning of the reign [1522] to this jiyou year [1549], ten examinations for selecting worthy men have been held. Distinguished and accomplished scholars have appeared in increasing succession: this is the full flowering of literary culture here. Looking now at the essays they submitted for examination, although each man's expression differs, they generally succeed in elucidating the sources of principle and encompassing past and present. Some possess a spirit embracing the traditions of Guan and Luo; some combine the refinement of Jiang and Zhe; some surpass Hu and Shu in grandeur; and some display a completeness of form…

title: 嘉靖二十八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
王畿者信藝文之都會華國之縟
觀也在昔輔臣楊士竒嘗謂長
材大器多出北方但鈍朴少文
視南士少讓爾廼今文采充蔚
炳乎煥焉儷美南國視士竒所
對之時不同矣抑長材大器以
致之用者不知視昔何如也
===
國家設科取士匪以其文亦欲因
文以考實繇言以知人耳爾多
士登名薦書裒然
帝畿之選或四方之良行且漸逵
亨衢服有官政尚其惇本崇質
充厥材猷而措之事業于以光
助太平純終令聞毋使質爲文
alt_text:
王畿者信藝文之都會華國之縟
觀也在昔輔臣楊士奇嘗謂長
材大器多出北方但鈍朴少文
視南士少讓爾迺今文采充蔚
炳乎煥焉儼美南國視士奇所
對之時不同矣抑長材大器以
致之用者不知視昔何如也
===
國家設科取士匪以其文亦欲因
文以考實繇言以知人耳爾多
士登名薦書裒然
帝畿之選甙四方之良行且漸逵
亨衢服有官政尚其惇本崇質
充厥材猷而措之事業于以光
助太平純終領聞毋使質爲文
punctuated:
王畿者，信藝文之都會、華國之縟觀也。在昔，輔臣楊士竒嘗謂：「長材大器多出北方，但鈍朴少文，視南士少讓爾。」廼今文采充蔚，炳乎煥焉，儷美南國，視士竒所對之時不同矣。抑長材大器，以致之用者，不知視昔何如也？

國家設科取士，匪以其文，亦欲因文以考實，繇言以知人耳。爾多士登名薦書，裒然帝畿之選，或四方之良，行且漸逵亨衢，服有官政。尚其惇本崇質，充厥材猷，而措之事業，于以光助太平，純終令聞，毋使質爲文
translation_en:
…the royal domain. Truly, this is a gathering place of literary accomplishment, a splendid spectacle that adorns the realm. In former times, Grand Secretary Yang Shiqi once said: “Men of outstanding talent and great capacity mostly come from the north; but they are unpolished and plain, with little literary refinement, and in this respect yield somewhat to southern scholars.” Now, however, literary brilliance flourishes in abundance, radiant and resplendent, matching the beauty of the south. Things are different from the time when Shiqi gave that response. Yet how those who put outstanding talent and great capacity to practical use compare with their predecessors, I do not know.

The state establishes examinations to select scholars not merely for their literary ability: it also wishes to examine their substance through their writing and to know the men through their words. You scholars whose names appear in the recommendation register stand distinguished as the chosen men of the imperial domain, or as worthy men from the four quarters. Soon you will advance along the broad road of success and undertake the duties of government office. May you strengthen your foundations, esteem substance, develop your talents and plans to the full, and apply them in practical achievements. Thus may you lend lustre and support to the age of peace and preserve your good reputation unsullied to the end. Do not allow substance to be subordinated to literary refinement…

title: 嘉靖二十八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
勝行以言浮庶於
今日求賢之意為無負矣矧
聖天子一德格
天至誠孚洽雨雪豐穰隨
蘄輒應
鴻名顯錫瑞穀效靈而
籲俊
===
===
賚弼又當孚感之會則共臣而敬
應對
昌期而樹風聲宜有以先天下矣
昔宋臣范仲淹嘗識富弼張方
平於舉子中厥後二子相業俱
顯君子以為知人爾諸士生逢
堯舜平居閎議固將以稷契自期待

勝行以言浮庶於
今日求賢之意爲無負矣矧
聖天子一德格
天至誠孚治雨雪豐穰隨
靳輙應
鴻名顯錫瑞穀效靈而
籲俊
===
賚弼又當孚感之會則共臣而敬
應對
昌期而樹風聲宜有以先天下矣
昔宋臣范仲淹嘗識富弼張方
平於舉子中厥後二子相業俱
顯君子以爲知人爾諸士生逢
堯舜平居閟議固將以稷契自期待
punctuated:
勝，行以言浮，庶於今日求賢之意為無負矣。矧聖天子一德格天，至誠孚洽，雨雪豐穰，隨蘄輒應；鴻名顯錫，瑞穀效靈，而籲俊賚弼，又當孚感之會，則共臣而敬應，對昌期而樹風聲，宜有以先天下矣。
昔宋臣范仲淹嘗識富弼、張方平於舉子中，厥後二子相業俱顯，君子以為知人。爾諸士生逢堯舜，平居閎議，固將以稷契自期待
translation_en:
…overcome by literary ornament, or conduct made superficial by words; thus you may avoid disappointing the intention behind today’s search for worthy men. Moreover, the sagely Son of Heaven reaches Heaven through his undivided virtue, and his utmost sincerity inspires trust far and wide. Rain, snow, and abundant harvests answer his prayers whenever offered; illustrious titles are manifestly bestowed, and auspicious grain displays its numinous power. The summons to outstanding men and the bestowal of worthy assistants likewise coincide with this meeting of sincerity and response. You should therefore respond reverently as ministers [?], establish an exemplary reputation in this flourishing age, and take the lead for all under Heaven.
Formerly, the Song minister Fan Zhongyan recognized Fu Bi and Zhang Fangping among the examination candidates. Later, both distinguished themselves through their achievements as chief councillors, and gentlemen considered Fan a discerning judge of men. You scholars have been born under rulers like Yao and Shun; in the lofty discussions of your daily lives, you surely aspire to emulate Ji and Xie…

title: 嘉靖二十八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
宋人勿論也然自獻成信茲實
階之其或媮名爽實竟自負於
明時則不惟虞廷之棄且為二子
之羞主司者知人之責視之仲
淹亦有餘愧臣不佞敬以相成
之義與諸士共勗之
翰林院侍講康大和謹序
alt_text:
宋人勿論也然自獻成信茲實
階之其或婾名爽實竟自負於
明時則不惟虞廷之棄且為二子
之羞主司者知人之責視之仲
淹亦有餘愧〔臣〕不佞敬以相成
之義與諸士共朂之
翰林院侍　講康〔大和〕謹序
punctuated:
宋人勿論也。然自獻成信，茲實階之。其或媮名爽實，竟自負於明時，則不惟虞廷之棄，且為二子之羞。主司者知人之責，視之仲淹，亦有餘愧。臣不佞，敬以相成之義，與諸士共勗之。
翰林院侍講康大和謹序。
translation_en:
…the men of the Song need not be discussed. Yet presenting yourselves and making good your sincerity truly begin with this step. Should any of you obtain a reputation unworthily while falling short in substance, ultimately failing yourselves in this enlightened age, you would not only be cast aside by the court of Shun but also bring shame upon those two men. Those presiding over the examination, charged with recognizing worthy men, would likewise have ample cause for shame when measured against Fan Zhongyan. I, your unworthy servant, respectfully offer this exhortation to all you scholars and to myself, in the spirit of helping one another achieve fulfillment.
Preface respectfully composed by Kang Dahe, Expositor of the Hanlin Academy.

title: 嘉靖二十八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
嘉靖二十八年順天府鄉試
提調官
通議大夫順天府府尹胡奎〔應文江西峽江縣人辛巳進士〕
順天府府丞竇一桂〔元方山西武鄉縣人丙戌進士〕
考試官
翰林院侍講康大和〔原中福建莆田縣人乙未進士〕
右春坊右賛善兼翰林院檢討閻樸〔文甫山西榆次縣人壬辰進士〕
同考試官
吏部文選清吏司辦事進士李詩〔以興四川江津縣人丁未進士〕
===

Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination, the twenty-eighth year of Jiajing (1549)

Proctors

Hu Kui, Grand Master for Thorough Counsel and Prefect of Shuntian Prefecture, had the courtesy name Yingwen and was from Xiajiang County, Jiangxi. He was a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) of the xinsi year.

Dou Yigui, Vice Prefect of Shuntian Prefecture, had the courtesy name Yuanfang and was from Wuxiang County, Shanxi. He was a metropolitan graduate of the bingxu year.

Examiners

Kang Dahe, Expositor in the Hanlin Academy, had the courtesy name Yuanzhong and was from Putian County, Fujian. He was a metropolitan graduate of the yiwei year.

Yan Pu, Right Mentor in the Right Secretariat of the Heir Apparent and concurrently an Examining Editor in the Hanlin Academy, had the courtesy name Wenfu and was from Yuci County, Shanxi. He was a metropolitan graduate of the renchen year.

Associate Examiners

Li Shi, a metropolitan graduate assigned to duties in the Bureau of Personnel Appointments of the Ministry of Personnel, had the courtesy name Yixing and was from Jiangjin County, Sichuan. He was a metropolitan graduate of the dingwei year.

Yang Yingyuan, Prefectural Judge of Ningguo Prefecture, Zhili, had the courtesy name Boren and was from Xiaoshan County, Zhejiang. He was a metropolitan graduate of the jiachen year.

Luo Wenwei, Magistrate of Linhuai County in Fengyang Prefecture, Zhili, had the courtesy name Bianfu and was from Qijiang County, Sichuan. He was a metropolitan graduate of the jiachen year.

Chen Shan, Magistrate of Tongcheng County in Anqing Prefecture, Zhili, had the courtesy name Sijing and was from Qiantang County, Zhejiang. He was a metropolitan graduate of the xinchou year.

Feng Chaoyong, Instructor at the Confucian School of Tunliu County in Lu’an Prefecture, Shanxi, had the courtesy name Ruji and was from Lintong County, Shaanxi. He was a tribute student (gongshi) of the dingyou year.

Qiu Wu, Instructor at the Confucian School of Ningyang County in Yanzhou Prefecture, Shandong, had the courtesy name Chaohong and was from Wujin County, Zhili. He was a tribute student of the wuzi year.

Zhu Zuo, Instructor at the Confucian School of Jiande County in Chizhou Prefecture, Zhili, had the courtesy name Sizhong; he was registered in Haiyan County, Zhejiang, and was from Haining Guard. He was a tribute student of the jiawu year.

Lin Ting, Instructor at the Confucian School of Jiangyin County in Changzhou Prefecture, Zhili, had the courtesy name Kongcheng and was from Dongguan County, Guangdong. He was a tribute student of the jiawu year.

Zhang Bin, Instructor at the Confucian School of Jinxi County in Fuzhou Prefecture, Jiangxi, had the courtesy name Bangxian and was from Putian County, Fujian. He was a tribute student of the guimao year.

title: 嘉靖二十八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
第壹塲
四書
舜有天下選於衆舉臯陶不仁者遠矣湯
有天下選於衆舉伊尹不仁者遠矣
君子之所不可及者其唯人之所不見乎
頌其詩讀其書不知其人可乎是以論其
世也
易
直其正也方其義也君子敬以直內義以
===
方外敬義立而德不孤直方大不習无
不利則不疑其所行也
益動而巽日進无疆天施地生其益无方
凡益之道與時偕行
易簡而天下之理得矣
萬物出乎震震東方也齊乎巽巽東南也
齊也者言萬物之潔齊也離也者明也
萬物皆相見南方之卦也聖人南面而
聽天下嚮明而治蓋取諸此也坤也者

凡益之道與時偕行
易簡而天下之理得矣

聽天下嚮明而治蓋取諸此也坤也者
punctuated:
第壹塲

四書

舜有天下，選於衆，舉臯陶，不仁者遠矣。湯有天下，選於衆，舉伊尹，不仁者遠矣。

君子之所不可及者，其唯人之所不見乎！

頌其詩，讀其書，不知其人，可乎？是以論其世也。

易

直，其正也；方，其義也。君子敬以直內，義以方外。敬義立而德不孤。「直方大，不習无不利」，則不疑其所行也。

益，動而巽，日進无疆。天施地生，其益无方。凡益之道，與時偕行。

易簡而天下之理得矣。

萬物出乎震，震，東方也。齊乎巽，巽，東南也。齊也者，言萬物之潔齊也。離也者，明也，萬物皆相見，南方之卦也。聖人南面而聽天下，嚮明而治，蓋取諸此也。坤也者
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

When Shun possessed all under Heaven, he selected from among the multitude and raised Gao Yao to office, and those lacking benevolence withdrew. When Tang possessed all under Heaven, he selected from among the multitude and raised Yi Yin to office, and those lacking benevolence withdrew.

Is it not precisely in what others do not see that the gentleman is beyond their reach?

When reciting their poems and reading their writings, can one fail to know what sort of people they were? This is why one examines the age in which they lived.

Book of Changes (Yijing)

Straightness signifies correctness; squareness signifies righteousness. The gentleman uses reverence to make his inner self straight and righteousness to make his outward conduct square. When reverence and righteousness are established, his virtue does not stand alone. “Straight, square, and great: even without practice, nothing is unfavorable.” Thus he has no doubts about his conduct.

Increase (Yi): movement combined with yielding brings daily progress without limit. Heaven bestows and Earth brings forth; their increase is unrestricted. Every way of bringing increase proceeds in step with the times.

Through ease and simplicity, the principles of all under Heaven are grasped.

The myriad things emerge in Zhen; Zhen is the east. They come to completeness in Xun; Xun is the southeast. “Coming to completeness” means that the myriad things become fully and distinctly formed. Li means brightness: the myriad things all become visible to one another. It is the trigram of the south. The sage faces south to hear the affairs of all under Heaven, turning toward the light to govern; this practice is surely derived from this. As for Kun …

title: 嘉靖二十八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
地也萬物皆致養焉故曰致役乎坤兌
正秋也萬物之所說也故曰說言乎兌
戰乎乾乾西北之卦也言陰陽相薄也
坎者水也正北方之卦也勞卦也萬物
之所歸也故曰勞乎坎艮東北之卦也
萬物之所成終而所成始也故曰成言
乎艮
書
帝德廣運乃聖乃神乃武乃文
===
俾萬姓咸曰大哉王言又曰一哉王心克
綏先王之祿永底烝民之生
惇信明義崇德報功
明王慎德四夷咸賓
詩
十月穫稻為此春酒以介眉壽
瞻彼洛矣維水泱泱君子至止福祿既同
君子萬年保其家邦
藹藹王多吉士維君子使媚于天子

===
詩
十月穫稻爲此春酒以介眉壽
瞻彼洛矣維水泱泱君子至止福祿既同
君子萬年保其家邦
藹藹王多吉士維君子使媚于天子
punctuated:
地也，萬物皆致養焉，故曰「致役乎坤」。兌，正秋也，萬物之所說也，故曰「說言乎兌」。戰乎乾，乾，西北之卦也，言陰陽相薄也。坎者，水也，正北方之卦也，勞卦也，萬物之所歸也，故曰「勞乎坎」。艮，東北之卦也，萬物之所成終而所成始也，故曰「成言乎艮」。

書
帝德廣運，乃聖乃神，乃武乃文。
俾萬姓咸曰：「大哉王言！」又曰：「一哉王心！」克綏先王之祿，永底烝民之生。
惇信明義，崇德報功。
明王慎德，四夷咸賓。

詩
十月穫稻，為此春酒，以介眉壽。
瞻彼洛矣，維水泱泱。君子至止，福祿既同。君子萬年，保其家邦。
藹藹王多吉士，維君子使，媚于天子。
translation_en:
…is earth. All things receive nourishment from it; hence the saying, “They are served by Kun.” Dui is mid-autumn, when all things rejoice; hence the saying, “They rejoice in Dui.” “They contend in Qian”: Qian is the trigram of the northwest, signifying yin and yang pressing against each other. Kan is water, the trigram of due north, the trigram of toil, to which all things return; hence the saying, “They toil in Kan.” Gen is the trigram of the northeast, where all things complete their ending and accomplish their beginning; hence the saying, “They reach completion in Gen.”

Book of Documents
The emperor’s virtue was vast and far-reaching: he was sagely and spiritually perceptive, accomplished in both martial and civil affairs.
Cause the people of all surnames to say, “Great are the king’s words!” and also, “Undivided is the king’s heart!” Thus you can preserve the blessings of the former kings and secure the people’s livelihood forever.
Cultivate trustworthiness and make righteousness manifest; honor virtue and reward meritorious service.
When an enlightened king attends carefully to his virtue, the peoples of the four quarters all submit as guests.

Book of Odes
In the tenth month we harvest rice and make this spring wine, to promote long life.
Look at the Luo River, its waters vast and flowing. The lord has arrived; blessings and emoluments gather upon him. May the lord live ten thousand years and preserve his house and state.
In abundance the king has many worthy men, whom the ruler employs and who are dear to the Son of Heaven.

季孫宿會晉侯、鄭伯、齊人、宋人、衛人、邾人于邢丘。襄公八年。

禮記
脩其教，不易其俗；齊其政，不易其宜。
樂者，敦和，率神而從天；禮者，別宜，居鬼而從地。故聖人作樂以應天，制禮以配地。
translation_en:
With leather-bound wheel hubs and ornamented crossbars, the eight carriage bells ring out. They come forward to present offerings; the mandate I have received is vast and great. From Heaven descends well-being, with abundant harvests in fruitful years. Come and draw near, come and partake of the offerings; send down blessings without limit.

Spring and Autumn Annals
In the sixth month, the Marquis of Qi came to present spoils from his victory over the Rong. Thirty-first year of Duke Zhuang. The people of Chu sent Yi Shen to present spoils of victory. Twenty-first year of Duke Xi.
In spring, in the first month of the royal calendar, the duke joined the Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Chen, the Marquis of Wei, the Earl of Zheng, the Baron of Xu, and the Earl of Cao in invading Cai. Cai collapsed. They then attacked Chu and encamped at Xing. Qu Wan of Chu came to make a covenant with the army; they concluded the covenant at Shaoling. Both passages are from the fourth year of Duke Xi.
The Heavenly King sent the Earl of Mao to confer a mandate upon the duke. First year of Duke Wen. In autumn, in the seventh month, the Son of Heaven sent the Earl of Shao to confer a mandate upon the duke. Eighth year of Duke Cheng.
Jisun Su met the Marquis of Jin, the Earl of Zheng, and representatives of Qi, Song, Wei, and Zhu at Xingqiu. Eighth year of Duke Xiang.

Book of Rites
Cultivate their instruction without changing their customs; bring their government into order without changing what suits their circumstances.
Music deepens harmony, leads the spirits, and accords with Heaven; ritual distinguishes what is fitting, gives the ghosts their places, and accords with Earth. Thus the sages created music to respond to Heaven and established ritual to correspond to Earth.

translation_en:
…When rites and music are clearly established and fully provided, Heaven and Earth fulfill their offices. The Son of Heaven forms a triad with Heaven and Earth; thus his virtue matches Heaven and Earth, benefiting all things alike. He shines alongside the sun and moon, his radiance illuminating all within the Four Seas and overlooking nothing, however small. Reciprocity benefits all under Heaven.

Second Session

Discourse: Utmost sincerity assists the transforming and nurturing processes of Heaven and Earth.

Edict, proclamation, and memorial 〔One question from among these [?]; the transcription is doubtful.〕
Compose an edict in the voice of a Han emperor ordering the ritual officials to encourage learning. 〔Fifth year of Yuanshuo.〕

A colleague renders decisions and signs official documents on another’s behalf.
An incumbent official erects a commemorative stele for himself without authorization.
Officers and soldiers desert while serving on campaign or on garrison defense duty.

第叁場
策五道

問：有一代聖明之君，必有輔弼之臣，聲應氣感，風動景從，蓋自古則然矣。我太祖高皇帝奮起淮甸，網羅豪傑，自癸酉肇建禮賢館，以處四方儒碩之士。時則於太平得一人焉，於鎮江得二人焉，於處州得四人焉，於金華得一人焉，又於諸暨得一人焉。當時講論經史，咨以時事，意則勤矣。不知草昧劻勷，日不暇給，何以聘召儒臣而親信如是耶？我成祖文皇帝嗣承洪業，簡任英賢，自癸未初開文淵閣，以處文學侍從之臣。時則以侍讀召入者吉水一人焉，以修撰召入者廬陵一人焉，以編修召入者建安一人焉、泰和一人焉，以檢討召入者新淦一人焉，

Deliberately committing an offense upon hearing that an imperial amnesty has been granted.
Implements, cotton cloth, and silk fabric that do not conform to statutory standards.

Third Session
Five Policy Questions

Question: Whenever an age has a sage and enlightened ruler, there must be ministers to assist him. They respond like answering sounds, resonate through their vital energies, and follow him as things stir before the wind and shadows follow forms. This has indeed been so since antiquity. Our Emperor Taizu Gao rose in the Huai region and gathered outstanding men into his service. In the guiyou year, he first established the Hall for Honoring the Worthy to accommodate eminent Confucian scholars from all quarters. At that time he obtained one man from Taiping, two from Zhenjiang, four from Chuzhou, one from Jinhua, and another from Zhuji. He discussed the classics and histories with them and consulted them about current affairs: his concern was truly earnest. Yet in those turbulent days at the founding of the dynasty, when each day scarcely afforded time enough for his tasks, why did he invite and summon Confucian ministers and show them such intimacy and trust?

Our Emperor Chengzu Wen succeeded to the great imperial enterprise and selected and appointed talented and worthy men. In the guiwei year, he first opened the Hall of Literary Profundity to accommodate literary ministers serving in attendance. At that time, among those summoned to enter service, there was one man from Jishui as Reader-in-Waiting; one from Luling as Senior Compiler; one from Jian’an and one from Taihe as Junior Compilers; and one from Xingan as Examining Editor…

永嘉一人焉南昌一人焉當時咨訪顧
問無間朝夕情則密矣不知代言之司
機密攸寓何以知諸臣能堪而拔擢如
是耶諸臣效忠宣力樹勳立業以酬知
遇者各有可言否耶我
聖天子中興禮樂寤寐人才尤重翰苑之儲嚴

共臣之願矣幸試言之
問三代無文人六經無文法古人之文如
風行水上無意而成者也自後世模倣

之六經論語文章之宗祖也乃有作太
玄作續經作法言作中說以擬之者昔
人已非之矣然觀漢書所載易有十三
家書有九家詩有六家春秋二十三家
punctuated:
永嘉一人焉，南昌一人焉。當時咨訪顧問，無間朝夕，情則密矣。不知代言之司，機密攸寓，何以知諸臣能堪而拔擢如是耶？諸臣效忠宣力，樹勳立業，以酬知遇者，各有可言否耶？我聖天子中興禮樂，寤寐人才，尤重翰苑之儲，嚴內閣之選。道化隆洽，玄澤汪濊，得人之治，振古有光。不知於二祖故事有默契乎否也？諸士抱藝觀光，且有共臣之願矣，幸試言之。

問：三代無文人，六經無文法。古人之文，如風行水上，無意而成者也。自後世模倣擬議之習興，而文始病矣。試與諸士評之。六經、《論語》，文章之宗祖也，乃有作《太玄》、作《續經》、作《法言》、作《中說》以擬之者，昔人已非之矣。然觀《漢書》所載，《易》有十三家，《書》有九家，《詩》有六家，《春秋》二十三家。
translation_en:
…one from Yongjia and one from Nanchang. At that time, he sought their advice and consulted them morning and evening without interruption: his relationship with them was indeed close. Yet the office charged with speaking on the emperor’s behalf was where confidential affairs were entrusted. How did he know that these ministers were equal to the task, and promote them in this way? Can something be said of how each repaid his recognition and favor by offering loyal service, exerting his strength, and establishing meritorious achievements?

Our sage Son of Heaven has revived rites and music, thinking of talented men both waking and sleeping. He attaches particular importance to cultivating a reserve of talent in the Hanlin Academy and rigorously selects members of the Grand Secretariat. His moral influence is exalted and all-pervading, his profound beneficence vast and abundant. His government, through obtaining worthy men, shines across the ages. Does it accord implicitly with the precedents of the Two Progenitors? You gentlemen have brought your literary attainments to behold the splendor of the realm, and moreover aspire to serve as ministers [?]. Please set forth your views.

Question: In the Three Dynasties there were no literary specialists, and in the Six Classics there were no rules of composition. The writings of the ancients were like wind moving over water, taking shape without deliberate intent. Only when later generations developed the habit of imitation and contrived emulation did writing begin to suffer. Let us consider this together, gentlemen. The Six Classics and the Analects are the ancestral sources of writing. Yet some composed the Supreme Mystery (Taixuan), the Continuation of the Classic (Xujing), the Model Sayings (Fayan), and the Discourses on the Mean (Zhongshuo) to emulate them. Earlier critics already condemned this. Yet, according to the History of the Han, there were thirteen schools for the Changes, nine for the Documents, six for the Odes, and twenty-three for the Spring and Autumn Annals…

title: 嘉靖二十八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
禮有十三家論語十二家皆自相擬議
各引一端篇分章列載籍浩博視之王
楊所作優劣何如耶抑於六經論語之
旨亦有得乎否也而君子所取者何耶
降是而下作對問者申寥廓之志作七
發者寓規諷之情此文章之流派云爾
而枝附影從比比而出曰賓戲曰客難
曰解嘲曰應譏曰達旨曰應問曰釋誨
曰抵疑曰釋譏曰客傲皆倣對問而作
===
者也曰七激曰七辨曰七依曰七命曰
七啓曰七厲曰七釋曰七說曰七諷皆
規七發而作者也其人其文亦可得論
其優劣歟比之於六經論語之旨相去
又何如耶夫秦漢以下士之名能文者
不外是數家而皆不能無議將六經論
語之外皆不可學耶諸士博極羣書必
有槩於中矣幸究言之以觀所尚
問一代之興必有一代之俗其來尚矣而

punctuated:
禮有十三家，論語十二家，皆自相擬議，各引一端，篇分章列，載籍浩博。視之王楊所作，優劣何如耶？抑於六經論語之旨，亦有得乎否也？而君子所取者何耶？降是而下，作對問者申寥廓之志，作七發者寓規諷之情，此文章之流派云爾。而枝附影從，比比而出，曰賓戲，曰客難，曰解嘲，曰應譏，曰達旨，曰應問，曰釋誨，曰抵疑，曰釋譏，曰客傲，皆倣對問而作者也。曰七激，曰七辨，曰七依，曰七命，曰七啓，曰七厲，曰七釋，曰七說，曰七諷，皆規七發而作者也。其人其文，亦可得論其優劣歟？比之於六經論語之旨，相去又何如耶？夫秦漢以下，士之名能文者，不外是數家，而皆不能無議，將六經論語之外皆不可學耶？諸士博極羣書，必有槩於中矣。幸究言之，以觀所尚。
問：一代之興，必有一代之俗，其來尚矣，而
translation_en:
…there were thirteen schools treating the Rites and twelve treating the Analects. All engaged in imitation and deliberation, each drawing upon one particular aspect, dividing their writings into sections and arranging them in chapters, producing a vast body of literature. How do their merits and shortcomings compare with the works of Wang and Yang? Did they, or did they not, attain some understanding of the purport of the Six Classics and the Analects? And what does the gentleman find worthy of acceptance in them?
In subsequent times, the author of Answering Questions (Duiwen) expressed his far-reaching aspirations, while the author of Seven Incitements (Qifa) conveyed his intention to admonish through indirection. These were simply branches of the literary tradition. Yet works attached themselves like branches and followed like shadows, appearing one after another: The Guest’s Jest (Binxi), The Guest’s Challenge (Kenan), Resolving Ridicule (Jiechao), Responding to Criticism (Yingji), Conveying the Purport (Dazhi), Answering Questions (Yingwen), Explaining Admonitions (Shihui), Countering Doubts (Diyi), Resolving Criticism (Shiji), and The Guest’s Taunts (Ke’ao). All were written in imitation of Answering Questions (Duiwen). Seven Stirrings (Qiji), Seven Discriminations (Qibian), Seven Reliances (Qiyi), Seven Injunctions (Qiming), Seven Enlightenments (Qiqi), Seven Exhortations (Qili), Seven Explanations (Qishi), Seven Persuasions (Qishui), and Seven Admonitions (Qifeng) were all written on the model of Seven Incitements.
Can the relative merits of these authors and their writings also be assessed? How far, in turn, do they stand from the purport of the Six Classics and the Analects? From the Qin and Han onward, men renowned for literary ability have belonged to no more than these few schools, yet none is beyond criticism. Does this mean that nothing outside the Six Classics and the Analects is worthy of study? You gentlemen have read widely throughout the whole range of books and must have formed judgments in your minds. Please discuss the matter fully, so that we may see what you esteem.
Question: Whenever a dynasty arises, it necessarily has customs particular to its age. This has long been so, yet…

translation_en:
…the Tribute of Yu (Yu gong) and the Office of Territorial Affairs section of the Offices of Zhou (Zhou guan) distinguish the mountains, rivers, and suitability of the lands of the Nine Provinces, yet leave this subject aside without discussing it. Why? Accounts of customs appear in the classics for the Three Dynasties and earlier, and in the histories for subsequent times. Which works record them in particular detail? Commentators say that the Eastern Han esteemed disinterested public criticism, so reputation and integrity were increasingly honored, while the Western Jin favored pure conversation, so ritual propriety and moral standards steadily declined. Could differences in the preferences of a particular age suffice to shape the customs of the whole realm? Yet an impartial examination of people of those times reveals some who did not entirely fit this pattern. Were there gentlemen whose conduct did not shift with prevailing influences and habits? Or did each person's attained character accord with his innate disposition, independently of customs? Examining changes through successive dynasties and taking the surviving records of past conduct as a mirror, so as to guard against partiality in one's preferences, is certainly an urgent task for scholars. Please set forth your views, so that we may see where your inclinations lie.
Question: Jia Shan of the Han said that Zhou had some eighteen hundred states. The people of the Nine Provinces supported the rulers of these eighteen hundred states; the rulers had wealth to spare, the people had strength to spare, and songs of praise arose. The flourishing unity of our dynasty far surpasses that of Zhou at its height, while the wealth and tax revenues of the southeast are renowned as a veritable sea of riches on land. There should be no danger of insufficiency. Yet in recent years both public and private resources have been depleted. Whenever funds are needed for government expenditure, the Minister of Revenue repeatedly reports that the treasury is exhausted. This…

其故何歟成周理財之法與今日耗財
之由可得言歟抑古今異宜不能槩論
也自周以下言利之臣代有其人其著
者漢有桑弘羊唐有劉晏宋有呂惠卿

智所可經畫則

其故何歟？成周理財之法與今日耗財之由，可得言歟？抑古今異宜，不能槩論也？自周以下，言利之臣代有其人，其著者，漢有桑弘羊，唐有劉晏，宋有呂惠卿，皆有意於足國者也。而三君者卒不聞收富庶之效，豈理財之法視成周亦有間歟？觀漢史載句踐之治越也，用計然之策，坐致富強。其臣范蠡又謂計然之策七，越用其五而霸。不知當時并其七而用之，又當何如也？視之漢唐宋言利之臣，亦有優劣否耶？今其術具在，試舉而行之於今，可乎？若曰天下之大，非私智所可經畫，則今日理財之道、足國之方，又將何以處之耶？此時務之最急者，幸明言之，將以轉聞於上。

問：夷狄爲中國患，自古已然，顧吾所以禦
translation_en:
…what is the reason for this? Can you explain the methods of financial administration under the Zhou at its height and the causes of financial depletion today? Or do ancient and present circumstances call for different measures, making a general discussion impossible? Since the Zhou, every age has had ministers who advocated ways of increasing revenue. Among the prominent ones were Sang Hongyang of the Han, Liu Yan of the Tang, and Lü Huiqing of the Song, all of whom intended to make the state financially sufficient. Yet none of these three men is ultimately known to have achieved wealth and prosperity. Could their methods of financial administration have fallen short of those of the Zhou at its height?

We read in the Han histories that, in governing Yue, Goujian employed Ji Ran’s policies and thereby attained wealth and strength with ease. His minister Fan Li further said that Ji Ran had seven policies, of which Yue employed five and attained hegemony. What would have happened had all seven been employed at that time? How do they compare in merit with the policies of the ministers who advocated increasing revenue under the Han, Tang, and Song? These methods are all still available today: could we try adopting and implementing them now? If it is said that the vast realm cannot be planned and managed through one person’s wisdom alone, then how should we address the methods of financial administration and the means of making the state financially sufficient today? This is the most urgent matter of present affairs. Please explain it clearly, so that your views may be conveyed to His Majesty.

Question: That the Yi and Di have caused trouble for China has been so since antiquity; the issue lies in how we defend against…

title: 嘉靖二十八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
之者何如耳昔人謂周得中策漢得下
策秦無策又有謂周得上策秦得中策
漢無策其果然歟我
太祖高皇帝驅掃胡元餘孽殆盡
成祖文皇帝親御六飛窮搜荒磧
二聖神武威靈昭播寰宇不審當時所得者何
策可遡而知歟抑于前代之策有相脗
合否也邇來北虜鴟張擾我疆圉
皇上宵旰圖惟務在安攘頃因災變
===
詔許陳言一時建議諸臣條具甚悉雖言人
人殊其大要不越壯地形增戍額而已
是果得其策之上歟抑外是二者而別
有說歟今塹山堙谷天險已成地形非
不壯矣懸金募士尺籍既盈戍額非不
增矣而犬羊無厭方且伺隙近地猶未
絕其南牧之心兵法曰無恃其不來恃
吾有以待之此其計將安出也諸士子
生長燕趙習聞虜情其於制御之畧蓋

punctuated: 之者何如耳。昔人謂周得中策，漢得下策，秦無策；又有謂周得上策，秦得中策，漢無策。其果然歟？我太祖高皇帝驅掃胡元餘孽殆盡，成祖文皇帝親御六飛，窮搜荒磧。二聖神武威靈，昭播寰宇。不審當時所得者何策，可遡而知歟？抑于前代之策有相脗合否也？邇來北虜鴟張，擾我疆圉。皇上宵旰圖惟，務在安攘。頃因災變，詔許陳言，一時建議諸臣條具甚悉。雖言人人殊，其大要不越壯地形、增戍額而已。是果得其策之上歟？抑外是二者而別有說歟？今塹山堙谷，天險已成，地形非不壯矣；懸金募士，尺籍既盈，戍額非不增矣。而犬羊無厭，方且伺隙近地，猶未絕其南牧之心。兵法曰：「無恃其不來，恃吾有以待之。」此其計將安出也？諸士子生長燕趙，習聞虜情，其於制御之畧，蓋
translation_en:
…it is simply a matter of how we defend against them. Men of earlier times said that the Zhou adopted a middling strategy, the Han an inferior strategy, and the Qin had no strategy. Others said that the Zhou adopted the best strategy, the Qin a middling strategy, and the Han had no strategy. Was this indeed so? Our Emperor Taizu Gao swept away almost all the surviving remnants of the Mongol Yuan. Emperor Chengzu Wen personally rode forth in his imperial chariot drawn by six swift steeds, searching to the furthest reaches of the desolate deserts. The divine martial prowess and awe-inspiring might of these two sage rulers shone throughout the world. What strategies did they adopt at that time? Can we look back and ascertain this? Did their strategies accord in any respect with those of earlier dynasties?

Recently the northern barbarians have grown rampant and disturbed our frontiers. His Majesty deliberates from before dawn until late in the day, intent upon securing peace within and repelling enemies without. Recently, in response to calamities and anomalous events, he issued an edict inviting opinions. The officials who then offered proposals set them out in great detail. Although their views differed from person to person, their main points amounted to no more than strengthening defensive terrain and increasing garrison establishments. Does this truly constitute the best strategy? Or is there some other approach beyond these two?

Now mountains have been trenched and valleys filled, completing the natural defenses: the terrain has certainly been strengthened. Rewards have been offered to recruit soldiers, and the military registers are full: the garrison establishments have certainly been increased. Yet these dogs and sheep remain insatiable, watching for openings to approach our territory [?], and have still not abandoned their desire to pasture their horses in the south. The Art of War says: “Do not rely on their not coming; rely on our having the means to meet them.” What plan, then, should we devise? You candidates were born and raised in Yan and Zhao and have long heard accounts of the barbarians’ circumstances. As for strategies to control and defend against them, you presumably …

Four Books
“When Shun possessed all under Heaven, he selected from among the multitude and raised Gao Yao to office, and those lacking benevolence withdrew. When Tang possessed all under Heaven, he selected from among the multitude and raised Yi Yin to office, and those lacking benevolence withdrew.”
Comment by Associate Examiner Feng, Instructor: The transitions in wording and meaning are clear and fully developed, showing a deep grasp of how benevolence and wisdom depend upon each other. The conclusion discusses the way emperors and kings, ancient and modern, have governed, particularly revealing the writer’s learning and discernment. He is an excellent scholar.
Comment by Associate Examiner Zhang, Instructor: Most writers in this examination follow established conventions. This essay has a powerful, integrated style and outstanding insights. It is a choice composition and should be recorded as a model.
Comment by Associate Examiner Li, metropolitan graduate (jinshi): Its talent and spirit are outstanding; its language and reasoning are pure and correct. This truly is the finest composition in the examination.
Comment by Examiner Yan, Right Admonisher: Its statements are well grounded.
Comment by Examiner Kang, Expositor-in-Waiting: Its meaning is rich and enduring.
Consider how emperors and kings display wisdom in appointing men to office, and how all under Heaven are thereby transformed toward benevolence. When all under Heaven follow and are transformed, we can see how benevolence and wisdom depend upon each other. title: 嘉靖二十八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
嘗帝天下矣時則邁種厥德仁莫如皐陶也乃
疇咨四岳舉之於儔人之中而明刑弼教之責
於是乎付之夫皐陶之舉特以盡吾舉措之公
爾而天下觀焉皆將去其不如皐陶者就其如
皐陶者率德改行藹然親睦之風而淫朋比德
若驅而遠去者是其始也任賢勿貳天下稱其
明其既也從欲風動四方歸其化舜之帥天下
以仁也為天下得人而已舜何心哉式商受命
纘禹舊服湯嘗王天下矣時則天民先覺仁莫
===
如伊尹也乃聿求元聖舉之於儔人之中而左
右阿衡之責於是乎寄之夫伊尹之舉亦以盡
吾舉措之公爾而斯民勸焉皆將去其不如伊
尹者就其如伊尹者有耻且格翕然歸極之良
而舊染汙俗若驅而遠去者是其始也帝臣不
蔽天下稱其明其既也綏猷允殖兆民歸其化
湯之仁不徧愛人也急親賢而已湯何心哉是
則於知人之中而寓安民之惠方其舉也安得
不謂之智及其化也安得不謂之仁仁智之相

punctuated: 嘗帝天下矣。時則邁種厥德，仁莫如皐陶也。乃疇咨四岳，舉之於儔人之中，而明刑弼教之責於是乎付之。夫皐陶之舉，特以盡吾舉措之公爾，而天下觀焉，皆將去其不如皐陶者，就其如皐陶者，率德改行，藹然親睦之風，而淫朋比德若驅而遠去者。是其始也，任賢勿貳，天下稱其明；其既也，從欲風動，四方歸其化。舜之帥天下以仁也，為天下得人而已，舜何心哉？式商受命，纘禹舊服，湯嘗王天下矣。時則天民先覺，仁莫如伊尹也。乃聿求元聖，舉之於儔人之中，而左右阿衡之責於是乎寄之。夫伊尹之舉，亦以盡吾舉措之公爾，而斯民勸焉，皆將去其不如伊尹者，就其如伊尹者，有耻且格，翕然歸極之良，而舊染汙俗若驅而遠去者。是其始也，帝臣不蔽，天下稱其明；其既也，綏猷允殖，兆民歸其化。湯之仁，不徧愛人也，急親賢而已，湯何心哉？是則於知人之中，而寓安民之惠。方其舉也，安得不謂之智？及其化也，安得不謂之仁？仁智之相
translation_en:
…had ruled All under Heaven as emperor. At that time, none equaled Gao Yao in benevolence, for he diligently cultivated his virtue. Shun therefore consulted the Four Chiefs, raised him from among his fellows, and entrusted him with the responsibility of making punishments clear to support moral instruction. In raising Gao Yao, he sought only to exercise complete impartiality in appointing and dismissing men. Yet all the world watched: everyone would abandon whatever in themselves fell short of Gao Yao and cultivate whatever resembled him. They followed virtue and reformed their conduct; a spirit of affection and harmony flourished, while wicked cliques and collusion in wrongdoing disappeared as though driven far away. At the outset, he employed the worthy without wavering, and all the world praised his discernment. Thereafter, people followed his wishes as things stir before the wind, and the four quarters submitted to his transforming influence. Shun led All under Heaven through benevolence simply by finding the right man for it. What private purpose did Shun have?

Shang received the Mandate and continued the dominion formerly held by Yu; Tang had ruled All under Heaven as king. At that time, none equaled Yi Yin in benevolence: he was one of Heaven’s people who had awakened to understanding before others. Tang therefore sought out this great sage, raised him from among his fellows, and entrusted him with the responsibility of assisting the ruler as chief minister, the A-heng. In raising Yi Yin, he too sought only to exercise complete impartiality in appointing and dismissing men. Yet the people were encouraged by this: everyone would abandon whatever in themselves fell short of Yi Yin and cultivate whatever resembled him. They acquired a sense of shame and rectified themselves, united in the goodness of turning toward the highest standard, while the corrupt customs that had long tainted them disappeared as though driven far away. At the outset, he made Yi Yin his minister without allowing his worth to remain obscured, and all the world praised his discernment. Thereafter, the way of peaceful government truly took root, and the myriad people submitted to his transforming influence. Tang’s benevolence did not consist in loving every person individually; he simply made drawing close to the worthy his urgent concern. What private purpose did Tang have?

Thus, within discerning men’s worth lay the beneficence of bringing peace to the people. At the moment of appointment, how could this fail to be called wisdom? Once its transforming influence had taken effect, how could this fail to be called benevolence? The mutual relationship between benevolence and wisdom…

translation_en:
…Such is the way benevolence and wisdom work together. Chi can now grasp for himself what the Master meant. Yet was this way exemplified only by Shun and Tang? Before them, Yao raised Shun to office, and the transforming influence that brought harmony to the age was accomplished. After them, King Wu raised Taigong to office, and the achievement of lasting peace became manifest. Drawing on both benevolence and wisdom, employing worthy men to secure good government: the way by which emperors and kings, past and present, govern all under Heaven extends no further than this. Ah! Is this something that only Fan Chi ought to understand?

“Is what makes the gentleman beyond others’ reach precisely what other people do not see?”

Comment by Associate Examiner Lin, Instructor: This composition elucidates the work of self-examination; everything flows from the writer’s own heart. He is someone who has long devoted himself to investigating human nature and Heaven’s mandate. I record it in celebration of having found a worthy man.

Comment by Associate Examiner Chen, District Magistrate: Its elucidation of the meaning of vigilance when alone is earnest, precise, and thorough.

Comment by Examiner Yan, Right Mentor: It perceptively conveys the gentleman’s work of scrutiny in action [?], a level that shallow learning cannot attain.

Comment by Examiner Kang, Expositor: Its language and reasoning are clear and lucid.

How could others match him in this? The final chapter of the Doctrine of the Mean quotes the Book of Poetry to discuss vigilance when alone. It is as though it said: the gentleman’s intention is fully encompassed by cultivating himself; the work of cultivating himself is fully encompassed by vigilance when alone. Thus the gentleman…

title: 嘉靖二十八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
子者性同天命之懿而至德淵微眾人無以喻
其妙道率彝倫之常而至神功化百姓無以與
其能是非天之獨厚於君子而君子之求以異
於人也亦非善于君子乎私屬而人于君子乎
私與也唯於其獨者加之意而已盖潛伏之地
若隱微而難知事理之幾則顯明而易辨眾人
以爲人所不見而忽之君子以爲已所特見而
謹之念慮方萌儼乎眾目之所視神明獨覺凛
乎上帝之是臨察利善之端而惟恐其自欺不
===
敢以怠心乘之也嚴天人之介而務求其自慊
不敢以私念雜之也此固爲已之實學君子之
所不可及者如斯而已否則狥外爲人其心亦
猶夫人耳何以爲君子哉抑是義也雖學者入
德之始事要之帝王相傳心法之要亦不外此
盖一念敬肆人之聖狂世之治忽實基之是故
明王純心體道恒致慎於幽微始於敬天勤民
極於位天地育萬物皆自吾心推之耳故曰有
天德便可語王道其要只在謹獨

translation_en:
…the gentleman shares the excellence of the nature bestowed by Heaven, yet his consummate virtue is so deep and subtle that ordinary people cannot comprehend its marvels. His way follows the constant norms of human relationships, yet his supremely spiritual power to accomplish and transform is such that the common people cannot match his capacities. This is not because Heaven favors the gentleman alone, or because the gentleman seeks to distinguish himself from others. Nor does goodness attach itself exclusively to the gentleman, or do people accord him their approval out of partiality. He merely gives particular attention to himself when alone.

The hidden recesses may seem obscure and difficult to know, yet the incipient workings of the principles of affairs are manifest and easy to distinguish. Ordinary people neglect them because others cannot see them; the gentleman is watchful over them because he alone can see them. When thoughts first arise, he is solemn, as though all eyes were upon him. When his spiritual awareness alone perceives them, he is awed, as though the Lord on High were looking down upon him. He scrutinizes the beginnings of benefit and goodness [?], fearing only that he might deceive himself, and dares not let a negligent mind intrude. He strictly maintains the boundary between Heaven’s principle and human desires, striving to be satisfied in his own conscience, and dares not mingle selfish thoughts with it. This is indeed the practical learning undertaken for one’s own moral cultivation. What makes the gentleman impossible to equal amounts simply to this. Otherwise, if he pursued outward things for the sake of others’ approval, his mind would be just like anyone else’s. How could he be a gentleman?

Moreover, although this principle is the learner’s first task in entering into virtue, the essentials of the teaching of the mind transmitted from one emperor or king to another ultimately extend no further. For whether a single thought is reverent or unrestrained is the very foundation of whether a person becomes a sage or a fool, and whether the world is well governed or falls into disorder. Thus the enlightened king makes his mind pure and embodies the Way, constantly exercising caution in what is hidden and subtle. Beginning with reverence for Heaven and diligent care for the people, and reaching as far as establishing Heaven and Earth in their proper places and nurturing the myriad things, all this is simply an extension of what is within his own mind. Hence the saying: “With Heaven’s virtue, one may then speak of the kingly Way.” Its essential point lies solely in vigilance when alone.

君子之友古人也，必因言而稽其行焉。夫行者，言之實也。君子既觀其言，又稽其行，取善寧有窮乎？孟子告萬章，若曰：友盡於一世，固足以徵進善之功，而或限於一時，亦非所以廣無方之益，則進而尚論於古也，當何如哉？彼溫柔敦厚，古人之言寓於詩也，則嘗誦其詩矣，而國風雅頌之音，已得於吟咏之素；疏通知遠，古人之言寓於書也，則嘗讀其書矣，而典謨訓誥之旨，亦得於玩索之餘。然所知者言爾，而為人之實非
translation_en:
“To recite their poems and read their writings without knowing what sort of people they were—is that acceptable? Thus one examines the age in which they lived.”

Associate Examiner Luo, County Magistrate, comments: “Most candidates addressing this topic in the examination hall have misplaced their emphasis. For elegant diction and lucid reasoning, none surpasses this essay. It truly deserves a high recommendation.”
Associate Examiner Yang, Prefectural Judge, comments: “Its elaboration of the examination of their age is precise. This is someone who has devoted his mind to the ancients.”
Examiner Yan, Right Companion to the Heir Apparent, comments: “Clear and polished, expansive and penetrating [?].”
Examiner Kang, Expositor, comments: “Words that fully grasp the principle.”

When a gentleman befriends the ancients, he must use their words to investigate their conduct. Conduct is the substance of words. Once the gentleman has considered their words and also investigated their conduct, how could there be any end to the good he draws from them? Mencius spoke to Wan Zhang as if to say: To befriend all the worthy people of one’s own age can certainly demonstrate progress in goodness. Yet to remain confined to a single period is no way to extend the benefits of an unrestricted pursuit. How, then, should one proceed to reach back and consider the ancients? Gentleness, warmth, sincerity, and generosity: the words of the ancients embodying these qualities reside in the Book of Odes. One has recited their poems, and through habitual chanting has already apprehended the sounds of the Airs of the States, the Elegantiae, and the Hymns. Breadth of understanding and knowledge of the distant past: the words of the ancients embodying these qualities reside in the Book of Documents. One has read their writings, and through reflection and inquiry has also apprehended the purport of its canons, counsels, instructions, and announcements. Yet what one knows is merely their words, and the reality of what they were as people is not …

title: 嘉靖二十八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
言之所能盡不知之可乎欲知其人矣而行事
之跡非世之所能拘不論之可乎故必仰止前
脩因言而觀其行作稽中德即事而論其心聖
之所以聖賢之所以賢吾究其實而已帝之所
以帝王之所以王吾探其蘊而已雖曰其人已
往也而布在方策宏規懿範固昭然可見矣雖
曰今人與居也而古人與稽精神默會固若共
一堂矣則論其世以知其人可不務乎夫尚論
乎古人也不徒知之以言而又知之以行則取
===
善以自益也不徒得之於言而又得之於行進
善其有窮乎噫友之道盡於是矣吾獨怪夫世
之誦詩讀書者不少也而尚友之道寥寥無聞
何邪蓋章句之習多而考德之功廢此齊桓所
以見誚於輪扁也然則不知其人不論其世而
動曰學古人者末矣孟子願學孔子而辭受進
退宛然家法所以告萬章者得非其自況者與
然千載之下讀孔孟之書而尚友者詎謂無其
人邪

punctuated: 言之所能盡，不知之可乎？欲知其人矣，而行事之跡非世之所能拘，不論之可乎？故必仰止前脩，因言而觀其行；作稽中德，即事而論其心。聖之所以聖，賢之所以賢，吾究其實而已；帝之所以帝，王之所以王，吾探其蘊而已。雖曰其人已往也，而布在方策，宏規懿範固昭然可見矣；雖曰今人與居也，而古人與稽，精神默會，固若共一堂矣。則論其世以知其人，可不務乎？夫尚論乎古人也，不徒知之以言，而又知之以行，則取善以自益也，不徒得之於言，而又得之於行，進善其有窮乎？噫！友之道盡於是矣。吾獨怪夫世之誦詩讀書者不少也，而尚友之道寥寥無聞，何邪？蓋章句之習多，而考德之功廢，此齊桓所以見誚於輪扁也。然則不知其人，不論其世，而動曰學古人者，末矣。孟子願學孔子，而辭受進退宛然家法，所以告萬章者，得非其自況者與？然千載之下，讀孔孟之書而尚友者，詎謂無其人邪？
translation_en: …cannot be fully encompassed by words. Can we leave it unknown? We wish to know the person, yet the traces of his deeds cannot be confined to his own age. Can we fail to discuss them? Thus we must look up to the worthy men of old, observing their conduct through their words; we must examine their inner virtue, considering their hearts through their deeds. What makes a sage a sage and a worthy man worthy—I seek only to investigate its substance. What makes a supreme sovereign a supreme sovereign and a true king a true king—I seek only to explore its underlying meaning. Though these men have passed away, their grand precedents and admirable examples are recorded in books and remain clearly visible. Though we live among people of the present, we examine ourselves against the ancients; in silent communion of spirit, it is indeed as though we shared a single hall. Can we neglect, then, to discuss their age in order to know the men? When we reach back to discuss the ancients, we know them not only through their words but also through their conduct. Accordingly, when we draw upon their goodness to improve ourselves, we gain not only from their words but also from their conduct. Could there be any limit to our advance in goodness? Ah! The way of friendship finds its fullest expression here. I find it strange that, although there are many in the world who recite the Book of Poetry and read the Book of Documents, so little is heard of the practice of reaching back to befriend the ancients. Why is this? It is because the study of textual divisions and sentences flourishes, while the work of examining virtue is neglected. This is why Duke Huan of Qi was reproached by the wheelwright Bian. Thus those who neither know the men nor discuss their age, yet constantly claim to emulate the ancients, attend only to superficialities. Mengzi wished to emulate Kongzi, and in declining or accepting gifts, entering service or withdrawing, he followed what was recognizably the tradition of that master's school. Could what he told Wan Zhang not have been a description of himself? Yet, a thousand years later, can it be said that there are none who read the writings of Kongzi and Mengzi and reach back to befriend them?

文言申坤六二，必原其德之所以大而化也。夫德至化而極也，然非君子之善學，亦何以致是哉？文言之意盖曰：德非學無以成，行非德無以妙。坤之六二，固得坤道之純而備直方之德矣。然所謂直者，言乎其正也，而中存之實有以植萬化之基；所謂方者，言乎其義也，而裁制之宜有以神感通之用。是皆吾之所固有者，而得之
translation_en:
Book of Changes

“Straightness signifies correctness; squareness signifies righteousness. The gentleman uses reverence to make his inner self straight and righteousness to make his outward conduct square. When reverence and righteousness are established, his virtue is not isolated. ‘Straight, square, and great: without practice, nothing is unfavorable’ means that he has no doubts about his conduct.”

Associate Examiner Lin, School Instructor, comments: “Concise, clear, pure, and correct. Only someone deeply versed in the learning of reverence and righteousness could attain this. It should be recorded as a model.”

Associate Examiner Chen, District Magistrate, comments: “Students gain no personal understanding in their study of the two terms ‘reverence’ and ‘righteousness,’ so their discussions are often disjointed. This composition is simple and direct, and amply reveals the writer’s self-cultivation.”

Examiner Yan, Right Mentor, comments: “Profound yet orderly: this is writing that elucidates principle.”

Examiner Kang, Expositor, comments: “Its understanding is precise and penetrating. This is an accomplished writer.”

In expounding the second, yin line of Kun, the Commentary on the Words of the Text must trace how its virtue becomes great and transformative. Virtue reaches its utmost in transformation; yet how could this be attained without the gentleman’s excellence in learning? The commentary’s meaning is, in effect: virtue cannot be perfected without learning, and conduct cannot attain subtle excellence without virtue. The second, yin line of Kun indeed possesses the purity of the Way of Kun and fully embodies the virtues of straightness and squareness. What is called ‘straight’ refers to its correctness: the substantial reality preserved within establishes the foundation of the myriad transformations. What is called ‘square’ refers to its righteousness: the appropriateness of its judgments and decisions renders its responsive interaction with things spiritually subtle. These are all things inherently possessed by us; yet our attainment of them …

title: 嘉靖二十八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
豈無自乎唯君子知養心莫如敬也則主敬以
直其内使渾然大中者適得吾體焉知制事莫
如義也則守義以方其外使物來順應者不失
吾常焉敬義既立則交養之益自不安於小成
充積之久將日就於逺大德何至於孤耶而辭
曰直方大不習无不利者盖以德之未盛則行
不能以無疑學之未充則德不能以無歉今則
造詣已極於精純而天德自泯於形迹易簡以
成能而全體之呈露固有不思而得者矣變通
===

何假於習而後利哉至是則德與聖人同歸而
化與坤道同運矣兹六二之所以為善學與抑
論學以成德敬義盡之矣而乾之九二則又以

全也敬義者語其學之要也他日夫子以克復
語顔子而以敬恕告仲弓人謂其有乾道坤道
之别其亦有見於是乎

punctuated:
豈無自乎？唯君子知養心莫如敬也，則主敬以直其内，使渾然大中者適得吾體焉；知制事莫如義也，則守義以方其外，使物來順應者不失吾常焉。敬義既立，則交養之益自不安於小成，充積之久將日就於逺大，德何至於孤耶？而辭曰：「直方大，不習无不利。」者，盖以德之未盛，則行不能以無疑；學之未充，則德不能以無歉。今則造詣已極於精純，而天德自泯於形迹，易簡以成能，而全體之呈露固有不思而得者矣；變通以盡利，而大用之顯行固有不勉而中者矣。又何假於習而後利哉？至是則德與聖人同歸，而化與坤道同運矣。兹六二之所以為善學與？抑論學以成德，敬義盡之矣，而乾之九二則又以學問寬仁言者，何耶？盖學問寬仁者，語其功之全也；敬義者，語其學之要也。他日夫子以克復語顔子，而以敬恕告仲弓，人謂其有乾道坤道之别，其亦有見於是乎？

萬物出乎震，震東方也；齊乎巽，巽東南也。
translation_en:
…could their attainment have no source? The gentleman alone knows that nothing surpasses reverence in nourishing the mind. He therefore makes reverence his guiding principle to straighten his inner life, so that undivided and perfect centrality finds its proper embodiment in him. He knows that nothing surpasses righteousness in managing affairs. He therefore holds to righteousness to square his outward conduct, so that, responding appropriately as things come, he does not depart from his constant principles. Once reverence and righteousness are established, the benefits of their mutual nourishment naturally prevent him from resting content with small accomplishments. Through long accumulation, he advances daily toward what is far-reaching and great. How could his virtue remain isolated?

The line statement says: “Straight, square, great: without practice, nothing is unfavorable.” This is because, while virtue is not yet abundant, conduct cannot be free of uncertainty; while learning is not yet complete, virtue cannot be free of deficiency. Now, however, attainment has reached the utmost refinement and purity, and heavenly virtue naturally leaves no visible trace. Through ease and simplicity he develops his capacities, and in the manifestation of the whole substance there is indeed an understanding attained without deliberation. Through adaptation and change he fully realizes what is beneficial, and in the manifest exercise of its great functioning there is indeed a rightness achieved without effort. What further need is there for practice before things become favorable? At this point, his virtue reaches the same destination as that of the sage, and his transforming activity moves together with the Way of Kun. Is this not why the six in the second place exemplifies skill in learning?

Yet, when discussing learning as the means of perfecting virtue, reverence and righteousness encompass it all. Why, then, does the nine in the second place of Qian speak instead of learning, inquiry, magnanimity, and benevolence? Learning, inquiry, magnanimity, and benevolence describe the full scope of the endeavor; reverence and righteousness describe the essentials of learning. On another occasion, the Master spoke to Yanzi of overcoming the self and returning to ritual propriety, while he instructed Zhonggong in reverence and reciprocity. People say that these teachings differ as the Way of Qian differs from the Way of Kun. Might they, too, have perceived this principle?

All things emerge in Zhen; Zhen is the east. They become ordered in Xun; Xun is the southeast.

translation_en:
…“Bringing into order” means that the myriad things become pure and orderly. Li means brightness: all things become visible to one another; it is the trigram of the south. The sage faces south to hear the affairs of All under Heaven, turning toward the light to govern; this is surely the source of that practice. Kun means earth: all things receive nourishment from it; hence the saying, “He brings service to completion in Kun.” Dui is autumn proper, in which all things rejoice; hence the saying, “He gives joy in Dui.” “He does battle in Qian”: Qian is the trigram of the northwest, signifying that yin and yang contend with one another. Kan means water; it is the trigram of due north, the trigram of toil, and the place to which all things return; hence the saying, “He toils in Kan.” Gen is the trigram of the northeast, where all things complete their end and accomplish their beginning; hence the saying, “He brings completion in Gen.”

Examiner Yan, Right Mentor, comments: “Skillfully draws together the meaning of the topic.”
Examiner Kang, Expositor-in-waiting, comments: “Fluent, clear, and cleanly expressed. Here is someone skilled at discussing the operations of creation.”
By observing the emergence and withdrawal of the myriad things, one can perceive that upon which the Sovereign on High rides. For the Sovereign on High is…

text:
妙萬物而爲言者也觀於物之出入而帝之所
乘有不可見乎夫子舉後天卦位而言之若曰
造化有自然之運生物有自然之機善觀帝者
必有驗於物矣是故帝出乎震固也而萬物亦
隨之以資始盖以震居正東則一陽初動而生
意自不能已焉帝齊乎巽固也而萬物亦隨之
以流形盖以巽居東南則一元效法而潔齊自
不可禦焉離者明之義而位於南方萬物際亨
嘉之會盖交相見矣聖人之所以南面而治者
===
不有取於此乎坤者地之象而順承天施萬物
荷滋息之恩盖向於實矣神化之所以致役乎
坤者不有徵於是乎兌屬正秋則發育之盛歡
欣交通而萬物適其性也所謂說言乎兌者此
耳乾居西北則陰陽之氣舒慘相攻而嚴凝肇
其令也所謂戰乎乾者此耳坎象爲水而位當

機於不息矣不曰成言乎艮耶夫物之出也帝

punctuated: 妙萬物而爲言者也。觀於物之出入，而帝之所乘有不可見乎？夫子舉後天卦位而言之，若曰：造化有自然之運，生物有自然之機，善觀帝者，必有驗於物矣。是故帝出乎震，固也，而萬物亦隨之以資始。盖以震居正東，則一陽初動，而生意自不能已焉。帝齊乎巽，固也，而萬物亦隨之以流形。盖以巽居東南，則一元效法，而潔齊自不可禦焉。離者明之義，而位於南方，萬物際亨嘉之會，盖交相見矣。聖人之所以南面而治者，不有取於此乎？坤者地之象，而順承天施，萬物荷滋息之恩，盖向於實矣。神化之所以致役乎坤者，不有徵於是乎？兌屬正秋，則發育之盛，歡欣交通，而萬物適其性也。所謂說言乎兌者，此耳。乾居西北，則陰陽之氣，舒慘相攻，而嚴凝肇其令也。所謂戰乎乾者，此耳。坎象爲水，而位當正北，則美利不言，歸其力於何有矣。不曰勞乎坎耶？艮居東北，而時介冬春，則終始循環，運其機於不息矣。不曰成言乎艮耶？夫物之出也，帝
translation_en:
…is spoken of in terms of the wondrous working of the myriad things. By observing things as they emerge and withdraw, can we fail to perceive that upon which the Lord on High rides? The Master explained this through the positions of the trigrams in the Later Heaven arrangement, as though saying: Creation has its spontaneous course, and the generation of things has its spontaneous impetus. Those who are skilled at observing the Lord on High must find corroboration in things.

Thus, the Lord on High assuredly comes forth in Zhen, and the myriad things likewise follow him, drawing upon it for their beginnings. For Zhen occupies due east: the single yang first stirs, and the impulse toward life cannot of itself cease. The Lord on High assuredly brings things into alignment in Xun, and the myriad things likewise follow him, unfolding into form. For Xun occupies the southeast: the primal origin manifests its patterns, and things cannot be prevented from becoming purified and aligned. Li means brightness and occupies the south. The myriad things encounter a conjunction of flourishing and excellence, and all become visible to one another. Does not the sage’s practice of facing south to govern derive from this? Kun images earth and compliantly receives Heaven’s bestowal. The myriad things receive the bounty of nourishment and growth and tend toward fruition. Is this not evidence of why the wondrous transforming power brings its service to fulfillment in Kun?

Dui corresponds to mid-autumn: growth and nurture reach their fullness, joy circulates, and the myriad things find satisfaction in their own natures. This is precisely what is meant by ‘giving delight in Dui.’ Qian occupies the northwest: the energies of yin and yang, mild and harsh, contend with one another, and bitter cold begins its sway. This is precisely what is meant by ‘doing battle in Qian.’ Kan images water and occupies due north: its fine benefits go unspoken, and to what claim of possession could its achievements be attributed? Is this not called ‘toiling in Kan’? Gen occupies the northeast, and its season lies between winter and spring: endings and beginnings follow one another in a cycle, its generative impetus operating without cessation. Is this not called ‘bringing things to completion in Gen’? Now, when things emerge, the Lord on High…

translation_en:
…the Sovereign’s manifestation in benevolence. The inward return of things is the Sovereign’s concealment in function. The Sovereign indeed embodies all things, leaving none out. Such is the subtlety of the trigram positions in the Later Heaven arrangement! Nevertheless, the Sovereign is one, and substance and function are present within movement and stillness. Yet the oppositions of the Earlier Heaven arrangement seem to present substance while omitting function, and the circulation of the Later Heaven arrangement to present function while omitting substance. Why is this? The Earlier Heaven arrangement concerns principle: it is how substance encompasses function. The Later Heaven arrangement concerns manifested workings: it is how function makes substance wondrously efficacious. Ultimately, the Way is also concrete things, and concrete things are also the Way: this is the constant unity of being and nonbeing. Thus, by contemplating the subtleties of the study of diagrams, one has already grasped more than half of the transmitted teaching of the minds of Fuxi and King Wen.

Book of Documents

“Cause the myriad families all to say, ‘Great indeed are the king’s words!’ and also to say, ‘Single indeed is the king’s heart!’ Then you will be able to preserve the blessings of the former kings and forever secure the livelihood of the multitude.”

Associate Examiner Luo, District Magistrate, comments: “This essay portrays Yi Yin’s heart of loyalty and loving concern so vividly that it seems present before one’s eyes. An excellent scholar! An excellent scholar!”

Associate Examiner Yang, Prefectural Judge, comments: “It expounds how unified virtue produces its confirming effects. Its language and tenor are pure and elegant; it can serve as a model.”

Examiner Yan, Right Mentor, comments: “It ably elucidates the intent of Yi Yin’s admonition to his ruler. For this reason, it has been selected for inclusion.”

title: 嘉靖二十八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
考試官侍講康批〔詞意懇惻蓋得伊尹之心者〕
大臣著一德之感乎民而其效為甚大也夫民
之稱頌未易得也而其效至於天人之交應焉
可不思所以致之耶伊尹進太甲而望之以此
若曰王之為德也博之以主善之功而約之於
協一之地其應果何如哉是故自其出令而言
謂之言言者心之聲也民於王言則以大哉稱
之布之於巽則曰申天下之命也發之於姤則
曰施四方之誥也萬姓雖殊而大哉之稱則協
===
感應之機若有以使之然矣自其出治之本謂
之心心者言之蘊也民於王心則以一哉稱之
成性存存若有見夫淵黙之秘也繼善亹亹若
可想其純一之真也萬姓雖異而一哉之稱則
同因言知心自有不容已者矣吾王之德其徵
諸庶民者如此由是上焉而天祿安受命孔固
而茀祿爾康也曆數無疆而天休滋至也蓋天
佑一德自有以克紹乎先王矣下焉而民生厚
九功惟叙而萬國咸寧也容保無疆而兆民允

Comment by Examiner Kang, Expositor-in-waiting: 〔The language and ideas are earnest and deeply felt; the writer has surely grasped Yi Yin’s heart.〕

The great minister made manifest how undivided virtue moves the people, and how exceedingly great its effects are. The people’s praise is not easily won; yet when the effects extend to a corresponding response from both Heaven and humanity, can one fail to consider how this is brought about? Yi Yin advanced his counsel to Tai Jia and held this expectation for him, as though saying: In cultivating virtue, Your Majesty broadens it through the effort of taking goodness as your guide and concentrates it upon unity. What response, then, will this produce?

Consider first the issuing of commands: this is called speech, and speech is the voice of the heart. Of the king’s words, the people exclaim, “How great!” When they are promulgated in the manner of the hexagram Xun, the Gentle, this is called reiterating commands to all under Heaven; when they are issued in the manner of the hexagram Gou, Encounter, this is called proclaiming instructions to the four quarters. Though the myriad families differ, they agree in their cry of “How great!” It is as though the workings of influence and response impel them to do so.

Consider next the source from which his governance proceeds: this is called the heart, and the heart holds what speech expresses. Of the king’s heart, the people exclaim, “How undivided!” As he continually preserves his perfected nature, they seem to perceive the mystery of its profound stillness; as he tirelessly carries goodness forward, they seem able to envision the reality of its purity and unity. Though the myriad families differ, they share the same cry of “How undivided!” Knowing his heart through his words, they cannot help responding thus. Such is the evidence of our king’s virtue among the common people.

From this, above, Heaven’s bounty is secured: his receipt of the mandate is firmly established, and abundant blessings bring him peace; his allotted succession of rule is without limit, and Heaven’s favor comes in ever greater measure. For Heaven assists undivided virtue, and thereby he can indeed carry on the legacy of the former kings. title: 嘉靖二十八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
殖也蓋民歸一德自有以光被乎九有矣夫天
祿安則所以庇下民者益深民生厚則所以荷
天祿者益固一德之效至是可以無愧烈祖之
訓矣抑因是而知大臣進戒之忠也夫修德固
難而一德尤難太甲始而敗度敗禮尹以先王
昧爽丕顯告之及其克終允德又以終始慎與
告之及茲歸政乃陳夫一德之功感應之效焉
其意懇惻而盡誠其言整暇而有序蓋其心以
厥后弗堯舜若撻于市故其忠愛無已有如此

殖也。蓋民歸一德，自有以光被乎九有矣。夫天祿安，則所以庇下民者益深；民生厚，則所以荷天祿者益固。一德之效至是，可以無愧烈祖之訓矣。抑因是而知大臣進戒之忠也。夫修德固難，而一德尤難。太甲始而敗度敗禮，尹以先王昧爽丕顯告之；及其克終允德，又以終始慎與告之；及茲歸政，乃陳夫一德之功、感應之效焉。其意懇惻而盡誠，其言整暇而有序。蓋其心以厥后弗堯舜，若撻于市，故其忠愛無已有如此。厥後太甲圖惟厥終，為有商之令主，其有得於斯言之訓與？

惇信明義，崇德報功。

translation_en:
…flourish. For when the people give their allegiance to undivided virtue, its radiance naturally extends throughout the nine regions. When Heaven’s bounty is secure, the protection afforded the common people grows deeper; when the people’s livelihood is abundant, the foundation for sustaining Heaven’s bounty grows firmer. With undivided virtue producing such results, one can stand without shame before the illustrious ancestor’s instructions.

Moreover, this reveals the loyalty with which a great minister offers admonition. Cultivating virtue is certainly difficult; keeping virtue undivided is harder still. When Tai Jia initially violated the standards and rites, Yi Yin admonished him by invoking the former king’s conspicuous virtue at daybreak. When he became capable of remaining truly virtuous to the end, Yi Yin again admonished him to exercise care from beginning to end. Now, upon returning the government to him, Yi Yin set forth the achievements of undivided virtue and the effects of the responses it elicits. His intention was earnest, compassionate, and wholly sincere; his words were composed, unhurried, and orderly. In his heart, if his sovereign failed to become a Yao or Shun, he felt as though he himself were being whipped in the marketplace. Such was his unceasing loyalty and affection. Thereafter Tai Jia gave thought to how he would finish and became an excellent ruler of Shang. Had he not benefited from the instruction contained in these words?

“Strengthen trustworthiness and make righteousness manifest; honor virtue and reward merit.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Luo, District Magistrate: Through powerful, profound, elegant, and vigorous language, this essay conveys the grandeur of imperial and royal action. It is among the very best essays interpreting the Book of Documents.

Comment by Associate Examiner Yang, Prefectural Judge: It sets forth the Zhou king’s policies of renewal in lucid, splendid, elegant, and disciplined language. Here is someone who has grasped the learning of ordering the world. Select it.

Comment by Examiner Yan, Right Mentor: The language is concise, yet no meaning is omitted. This must be the work of an accomplished writer.

title: 嘉靖二十八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
考試官侍講康批有文采有典則讀之灑然
勵俗而勸善者周王之所以治也夫俗不勵善
不勸治皆苟而已周王知所重焉其受丕丕基
也固宜且夫帝王之治天下莫不以敎化人材
爲先務故觀諸武王而知周道之興也是故人
君所以率下以成俗者有信與義也弗敦而明
之則忠信薄而大道隱吾見其俗之日敝矣武
王則以一道德同風俗固先王經綸之迹也我
可忘耶故於信則敦之協一以固羣情確乎無
===
妄之貞也義則明之大公以昭眾志煥乎藝極
之樹也蓋中孚以起信則俗不漓通變以宜民
則化不匱所以表正風俗之道豈其微哉人臣
所以事上而爲善者有德與功焉弗崇而報之
則植行阻而程能隳吾見其善之罔終矣武王
則以褒有德錄賢能固帝王之所繇昌也我可
廢耶故於德者崇焉明揚師錫隆晉接之恩也
功者報焉彤弓致饗昭大賚之典也蓋爵以馭
貴式彰王國之楨賞以酬勳益表社稷之隸所

Examiner Kang, Expositor, comments: “It has literary brilliance and conforms to established standards. Reading it leaves one refreshed.”

Spurring the improvement of customs and encouraging goodness were the means by which the king of Zhou governed. If customs are not improved and goodness is not encouraged, government is merely makeshift. The king of Zhou knew what deserved emphasis; it was indeed fitting that he should receive so vast a foundation. Moreover, emperors and kings, in governing All under Heaven, invariably make moral instruction and men of talent their foremost concerns. Thus, by looking at King Wu, we can understand the rise of the Way of Zhou.

Trustworthiness and righteousness are what a ruler uses to lead those below him and shape their customs. Unless he strengthens the former and makes the latter clear, loyalty and trustworthiness grow thin and the Great Way becomes obscured. I see that the people's customs would then deteriorate daily. King Wu, however, held that unifying moral principles and bringing customs into accord were indeed the achievements of the former kings in ordering the realm: “Could I forget them?” Thus he strengthened trustworthiness, fostering unity to secure the allegiance of the multitude, firm in the constancy of being without falsehood. He clarified righteousness, illuminating the aspirations of all through complete impartiality, splendidly establishing the highest standard [?]. Through inward sincerity he inspired trustworthiness, so that customs did not become debased; by adapting to change he met the people's needs, so that his transforming influence did not fail. Could the means by which he set an example and rectified customs have been insignificant?

Virtue and merit are what ministers employ in serving their ruler and doing good. Unless these are honored and rewarded, the cultivation of conduct is obstructed and the exercise of ability falls into neglect. I see that their goodness would then fail to endure. King Wu, however, held that praising the virtuous and employing the worthy and capable were indeed the means by which emperors and kings flourished: “Could I abandon them?” Thus he honored those possessed of virtue: he publicly raised up those recommended by the multitude and bestowed office upon them, magnifying the favor of receiving them in audience. He rewarded those possessed of merit: he conferred vermilion bows and held feasts, manifesting the institution of generous royal rewards. Through ranks he regulated the noble, thereby giving recognition to the pillars of the kingdom; through rewards he recompensed meritorious service, further distinguishing the servants of the altars of soil and grain. …is this not where the power to inspire the ministers lies? In this way, the people undergo a profound transformation in their customs, while the ministers provide the benefit of steadfast assistance. Government in which the ruler need only fold his hands thus develops by degrees. Moreover, when sovereigns found states and establish ruling houses, their conduct and bearing must greatly surpass those of ordinary men. Regulating affairs and disciplining the heart, receiving assistance and bringing achievements to fruition—these were how Tang succeeded the Xia. In succeeding the Shang, King Wu added lustre to Tang’s example. Thus the blessings of trustworthiness, righteousness, achievement, and virtue, extending over eight hundred years, were all King Wu’s legacy. The reason was that he heard the categories of the Great Plan from Jizi and received the admonitions of the Cinnabar Writing from Taigong: his learning as a sage had its own deep sources. Hence his mighty achievements were carried forward on a grand scale, standing foremost through the ages, beyond anyone’s reach. Ah, how splendid!

Examiner Yan, Right Admonisher, comments: Its account of the Zhou king’s intention to preserve good order is exceptionally earnest and thorough. The writer has, it seems, a deep understanding of the Odes.
Examiner Kang, Expositor-in-waiting, comments: Dignified and weighty, without superficiality: it vividly brings to mind the flourishing age of Chengzhou.
The poet praises the king for coming to the central capital and enjoying great blessings, thereby possessing the means to perpetuate his great enterprise. How essential are anticipating troubles and taking precautions—the way by which a ruler secures lasting peace and enduring good government! The Zhou king followed this way; how fitting that the poet praised him! This poem was composed by the regional lords to praise the Son of Heaven when he assembled them at the eastern capital to conduct military exercises. Its meaning is that the succession of order and disorder is a constant pattern in Heaven’s workings, while establishing order and preserving the state is an enlightened sovereign’s highest strategy.
Thus, look upon that capital at Luo: its origins reach far back. It was the Duke of Shao who laid the foundations of the mandate, and the Duke of Zhou who secured it. The royal city and the lower capital linked inner and outer regions; the Chan to the west and the Jian to the east gave the landscape its winding, flowing character. Look at its waters, so abundant, deep, and broad! When our lord arrives here, the configuration of the land serves to unite the people’s hearts, and the people’s hearts serve to consolidate Heaven’s mandate. Great ease and abundant prosperity are enjoyed together as the magnificence of his own person. Those whom Heaven assists are obedient to its order; those whom people assist are trustworthy. Blessings in their tens of thousands and hundreds of millions gather into good fortune arriving again and again. Have not his blessings and emoluments all come together?
Yet, dwelling at the center and planning great undertakings, he does not forget to cultivate military preparedness. 家邦蓋與今日無間也以萬國則咸賓以四夷
則來王由一世以觀百世而萬世之人心可知
也以一統則無虞以保定則孔固由今日以觀
後日而無窮之景祚可卜也則信乎東都講武
之行寔祈天永命之繫矣噫若周王者其知天

家邦，蓋與今日無間也。以萬國則咸賓，以四夷則來王，由一世以觀百世，而萬世之人心可知也；以一統則無虞，以保定則孔固，由今日以觀後日，而無窮之景祚可卜也。則信乎，東都講武之行，寔祈天永命之繫矣。噫！若周王者，其知天下之大計者哉！抑是詩之作，當在成康之世。觀周公戒成王，則曰：「克詰戎兵。」召公戒康王，則曰：「張皇六師。」是詩之意，頌而無謟，其有周召之志乎？傳世歷年，卒過其曆，其源流遠矣。《易》有之：「危者，安其位者也；亡者，保其存者也；亂者，有其治者也。」於戲！觀夫子繫《易》之意，而詩人稱頌之旨可識矣。

藹藹王多吉士，維君子使，媚于天子。

同考試官教諭馮批：詞懇而雅，氣和而莊，非忠愛素蓄者不能形容至此。宜錄以式。

同考試官教諭張批：老成典麗，氣象不凡。「媚天子」處尤講親切。子其亦王之吉士歟？
translation_en:
…his royal house and realm, surely with no difference from today. The myriad states will all submit as guests, and the peoples of the four quarters will come to acknowledge him as king. From one generation we may judge a hundred generations, and thus know the hearts of the people for ten thousand generations. With unity there will be no cause for anxiety; with preservation and stability, the foundations will be exceedingly firm. From today we may judge the days to come, and thus foretell an auspicious reign without end. Truly, then, the expedition to conduct military exercises at the eastern capital was bound up with praying to Heaven for an enduring mandate. Ah! A king such as this king of Zhou surely understood the great designs needed to govern All under Heaven!

Moreover, this ode must have been composed in the age of Kings Cheng and Kang. Consider how the Duke of Zhou admonished King Cheng: “Be able to put your military forces in order.” The Duke of Shao admonished King Kang: “Make the Six Armies imposing and illustrious.” This ode praises without flattery: does it not embody the aspirations of the Dukes of Zhou and Shao? As the dynasty passed through generations and accumulated years, it ultimately exceeded its allotted span; the sources of its longevity reach far back. The Book of Changes says: “Those in danger are those who feel secure in their positions; those who perish are those assured of their continued existence; those in disorder are those who presume they possess good order.” Ah! By considering the Master's meaning in the Appended Statements to the Book of Changes, we may understand the poet's intent in offering praise.

Abundant are the king's many worthy men; it is gentlemen whom he employs, who cherish the Son of Heaven.

Comment by Associate Examiner Feng, Instructor: The language is earnest and elegant; the tone, harmonious and dignified. Only someone who has long nurtured loyalty and devotion could portray these sentiments so fully. This should be selected for inclusion as a model.

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhang, Instructor: Mature, classically refined, and elegant, this writing has an exceptional bearing. Its treatment of “cherishing the Son of Heaven” is especially apt and heartfelt. Are you not yourself one of the king's worthy men?

詩人表賢才生世之盛，而有用世之忠焉。夫賢才之盛，固應運而生也，則夫用而效忠於君，亦其心之不容自已矣。召公以壽考福禄歆動王心，而進之以得賢自輔之益，若曰：「明主必待賢臣而弘功業，俊士亦俟明主以顯其德，君臣相遇而豈徒哉！」自今觀之，天地淳和之氣孕而為人物之精華，國家豐芑之仁衍而為人文之宣廱。曰馮曰翼，皆名世之賢也；若孝若德，皆庶常之吉也。賢才之多如此，亦顧用之何如爾。使其翕受敷施，而廣籲俊之公；服休服采，而應交如之會，則豈自負於明時哉！皆將曰：「君之事，吾事也。」罔不既厥心。又莫不曰：「吾之身，君身也。」不容以自重。進而盡忠焉，退而補過焉。所以事之者，事不同而媚同；父兄之臣誠愛宗廟，法度之臣
translation_en:
Associate Examiner Li, a metropolitan graduate (jinshi), comments: “The interpretation is refined and the wording precise: it conveys perfectly the loyal devotion of a veteran minister.”
Examiner Yan, Right Mentor, comments: “In interpreting the Poetry, warmth, richness, meticulousness, and coherence are prized. This composition approaches that standard.”
Examiner Kang, Expositor, comments: “Intimate, elegant, and harmonious: reading it can stir the heart.”

The poet celebrates the abundance of worthy talent born into the world, together with its loyalty in serving the age. Such an abundance of worthy talent certainly arises in response to the fortunes of the times; once employed, these men likewise cannot restrain their hearts from rendering loyal service to their ruler. The Duke of Shao moves the king’s heart with the prospect of longevity and blessings, then advances the benefits of obtaining worthy men to assist him. It is as though he were saying: “An enlightened ruler must await worthy ministers to enlarge his achievements; outstanding gentlemen likewise await an enlightened ruler to make their virtue manifest. Can the meeting of ruler and ministers be without consequence?”

Viewed from the present, the pure and harmonious vital force of Heaven and Earth nurtures the finest among men, while the state’s benevolence in cultivating talent—as luxuriant millet is nurtured—extends into the flourishing harmony of human culture. Those who provide support and those who give assistance are all worthies renowned in their age; the filial and the virtuous are all excellent men among the ordinary officers. With worthy talent so abundant, everything depends on how it is employed. Let them be received together and deployed widely, extending the impartiality of the call for outstanding men; let them undertake noble service and perform their duties, answering the occasion when ruler and ministers meet in accord. How could they then fail their own promise in an enlightened age?

They will all say, “The ruler’s affairs are my affairs,” and none will fail to exert his heart to the utmost. Again, all will say, “My person belongs to the ruler,” and will not permit themselves to hold their own persons too dear. Advancing into his presence, they exhaust their loyalty; withdrawing, they remedy his faults. The services by which they attend him differ, but their loving devotion is the same. Ministers who stand as fathers and elder brothers sincerely cherish the ancestral temple; ministers charged with laws and institutions …

哉故後世誦成王之治而歌召公之功不衰

誠愛社稷。所以媚之者，職不同而情同。所以然者，蓋愛君之心，彼固植乎其性，而效忠熈載，尤有感於其時。向使遺而不用，則恒相求而不相遇，將如愛君何哉？噫！大臣進戒之意淵矣！考之成周之世，野無遺賢，萬邦咸寧，而召公進戒，猶欲其得賢自輔，以爲壽考福祿之地。憂治世而危明主，老成忠愛之心固如此。觀《召誥》之作，拳拳於歷年之乆，近夏商之廢興，且以誠小民疾、敬德爲祈天永命之本，蓋與此詩之作異詞同旨。然則成王所以爲太平有道令主，豈無所自哉？故後世誦成王之治，而歌召公之功不衰。
