translation_en:
…truly love the altars of soil and grain. Thus, although their offices differ, the affection with which they serve their ruler is the same. This is because their love for their ruler is firmly rooted in their nature, while their fulfillment of loyal service and advancement of public affairs are especially inspired by the age in which they live. Had they been passed over and left unemployed, ruler and worthy men would continually have sought one another without meeting. How then could they have expressed their love for their ruler? Ah! Profound indeed was the intention behind the great minister’s admonition!

Consider the age of the established Zhou: no worthy men remained neglected in the countryside, and the myriad states were all at peace. Yet the Duke of Shao, in offering his admonition, still wished the king to obtain worthy men to assist him, thereby laying the foundation for longevity, blessings, and emoluments. To feel concern in an age of good government and apprehension for an enlightened ruler—such indeed is the loyal affection of a seasoned elder. In the Announcement of Shao, we see his earnest concern that the dynasty endure for many years. He draws on the relatively recent rise and fall of Xia and Shang, and makes sincere concern for the sufferings of the common people [?] and reverence for virtue the basis for praying to Heaven for an enduring mandate. Its wording differs from that of this poem, but its purport is the same. Was it, then, without any foundation that King Cheng became an excellent ruler who followed the Way and brought about great peace? Thus later generations have celebrated King Cheng’s government and sung the praises of the Duke of Shao’s achievements without cease.

Spring and Autumn Annals

“In the sixth month, the Lord of Qi came to present the spoils of victory over the Rong.” The thirty-first year of Duke Zhuang. “The men of Chu sent Yi Shen to present the spoils of victory.” The twenty-first year of Duke Xi.

春秋於伯主之遺俘也，卑詞以抑之；於望國之受俘也，諱詞以貶之。夫諸侯無相遺俘之禮也。齊急於功，魯怵於威，春秋抑而貶之，宜哉！且齊何為而獻捷于魯耶？桓公親伐山戎，諸侯賓服，于是獻俘于魯，所以誇之也。夫戎居荒服，既非畿甸之邦，雖嘗病燕，亦非門庭之寇。懸師而遠伐之，操之為已蹙矣。吾聞先王之於外夷也，負固而不服，則有文德之綏；序成而不至，則有聲罪之討。及其班師振旅，則告之天王而獻其功，禮也。今乃窮兵深入，張皇闢地之師，躬獻俘獲，誇示甥舅之國，此何為者耶？噫！苗民逆命，有舞干羽以格之者矣，不圖桓之昧乎此也。故抑之而書來獻，所以杜厲之階也，蓋如此。且宜申又何為而獻捷于魯耶？楚成伏兵圍宋，魯僖不與，至是歸俘于魯，所以脅之也。夫宋本上公，方主中國之盟，楚以夷狄，乃逞襲執之詐，以俘而獻於魯，橫逆亦已甚矣。吾聞先王之於隣國也，親

Comment by Examiner Kang, Expositor: “This writer is skilled at composing phrases and juxtaposing events. Include this answer.”

When a hegemon sends captives as a gift, the Spring and Autumn Annals uses belittling language to curb him; when an eminent state receives captives, it uses veiled language to disparage it. There is no ritual provision for regional lords to send captives to one another. Qi was impatient for achievement, and Lu was intimidated by force. How fitting that the Spring and Autumn Annals should curb and disparage them!

Why, then, did Qi present the spoils of victory to Lu? Duke Huan personally attacked the Shanrong, and the regional lords submitted to him. He then presented captives to Lu in order to vaunt his achievement. The Rong inhabited the remote outer zone, beyond the royal domains. Although they had troubled Yan, they were not invaders at Qi’s own gates. To send an army far afield to attack them was excessively impetuous. I have heard that when the former kings dealt with the outer barbarians, if they relied on their strongholds and refused submission, the kings pacified them through civil virtue; if an ordered relationship had been established but they failed to attend court, the kings proclaimed their offenses and mounted a punitive expedition. When the army returned and its ranks were put in order, they reported to the Heavenly King and presented their achievements. This accorded with ritual. Yet now Duke Huan exhausted his forces in deep incursions, ostentatiously deployed an army to expand his territory, and personally presented captives and booty, boasting before a state bound to his by marriage. What sort of conduct was this?

Alas! When the Miao people defied commands, there was one who brought them to submission through dances with shields and feathered plumes. Who would have expected Duke Huan to be ignorant of this? Thus the Annals curbs him by recording “came to present”: this was its means of blocking the steps leading to harmful excess.

And why did Yishen likewise present the spoils of victory to Lu? King Cheng of Chu laid an ambush and surrounded the ruler of Song; Duke Xi of Lu did not participate. At this point Chu sent captives to Lu in order to intimidate it. The ruler of Song held the exalted rank of duke and was then presiding over the covenant of the central states. Yet Chu, a barbarian state, brazenly employed the deceit of a surprise attack and seizure, and presented captives to Lu. Its violent defiance had gone much too far! I have heard that, in their dealings with neighboring states, the former kings befriended…

translation_en:
…the benevolent and maintain good relations with neighboring states, thereby showing kindness to the states on every side; relieve disasters and succor those in distress, showing due respect for the written commands. When the Yi and Di peoples throw the Xia realm into disorder, it is proper to request authorization from the Son of Heaven and undertake a punitive expedition. Yet now he calmly accepted Chu’s offering, his resolve to honor the king and repel the barbarians utterly gone; he stood by and watched Song’s distress, while no army stirred to punish the guilty. What conduct was this? Alas! When the western Lü brought tribute, there was someone who set forth the great principles of righteousness to turn it away. Who would have thought Duke Xi would be so blind to this? Thus, in recording the acceptance of the spoils of victory without mentioning Song, the text conceals Lu’s disgrace. Such is the reason. The principle is fully evident: when distant barbarians give no cause for conflict, one must not provoke hostilities on the frontier to seek military distinction; when the Yi and Di throw the Xia realm into disorder, one should uphold the great principles of righteousness and undertake a punitive expedition. From this we also learn of the failings of Qi and Song. Duke Huan of Qi and Duke Xiang of Song both presided as hegemons. In the campaign against Guzhu, Duke Huan indulged his appetite for warfare. Was Guan Zhong not at his side? At the meeting at Yu, Duke Xiang went with war chariots to meet Chu, willingly exposing himself to capture; the loyal counsel of Prince Muyi went unheeded. Can a state possibly dispense with employing worthy men to achieve good government? Alas! This is why the gentleman so deeply regrets the failings of these two hegemons.
In spring, in the first month of the royal calendar, the duke joined the Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Chen, the Marquis of Wei, the Earl of Zheng, the Baron of Xu, and the Earl of Cao in invading Cai. Cai collapsed. They then attacked Chu and encamped at Xing.
Qu Wan of Chu came to make a covenant with the army. They concluded the covenant at Shaoling. 〔Both passages are from Duke Xi’s fourth〕〔year.〕

考試官侍講康批：詞核義正，得聖人書法。
春秋於伯主用竒正之兵以攘外，必譏其專而序其績焉。此見桓之攘楚，事雖專而善有足錄者。觀春秋所書，功過豈容掩哉？楚自西周爲中國患久矣。齊桓主霸，銳意南征，始而侵蔡者竒也，而蔡潰；繼而伐楚者正也，而楚恐。及夫陘亭既次，屈完惠來，乃即召陵而盟焉。此一事也，春秋何以譏其專，復序其績耶？蓋自其專言之，人臣所明者義，功非所貴也。夫以楚之包茅不貢，王祭不供，不可以莫討也。桓苟以内安外攘爲心，而請命于周焉，其誰非之？乃專上行私，偕茲八國，威福之作，令不出於王朝；征討之加，兵不由於司馬。是猶父兄在堂，而子弟外徼生事也。有王者作，桓其能免乎？故書「遂伐楚」者，譏其專也。所謂以義正名，而教天下之忠，在是矣。自其績言之，盟主所務者德，力非所尚也。夫以楚之
translation_en:
…correct. Even if he were raised from the grave, he would surely be inwardly convinced.

Comment by Examiner Yan, Right Mentor: The passages assigning praise and blame show considerable skill in historical judgment.

Comment by Examiner Kang, Expositor: The wording is precise and the principles correct; it captures the Sage’s manner of recording events.

When a hegemonic lord employs unorthodox and orthodox military operations to repel external powers, the Spring and Autumn Annals invariably censures his unauthorized action while recounting his achievements. This is evident in Duke Huan’s campaign against Chu: although he acted on his own authority, there was good in what he did that deserved recording. Looking at what the Spring and Autumn Annals records, how could either his merits or his faults be concealed? Chu had long been a source of trouble for the central states, ever since the Western Zhou. Duke Huan of Qi, assuming leadership as hegemon, was determined to campaign southward. His initial invasion of Cai was an unorthodox operation, and Cai collapsed; his subsequent attack on Chu was an orthodox operation, and Chu grew afraid. After he had encamped at Xingting, Qu Wan graciously came to him, and they then proceeded to Shaoling and concluded a covenant. This was a single affair: why does the Spring and Autumn Annals both censure his unauthorized action and recount his achievements?

Viewed in terms of his unauthorized action, what a ruler’s minister must make manifest is righteousness; achievement is not what is prized. Since Chu failed to present its tribute of bundled thatch, leaving the king’s sacrifices without their supplies, it could not be left unpunished. Had Duke Huan set his heart on securing the interior and repelling external threats, and requested authorization from Zhou, who could have criticized him? Instead, he usurped his superior’s authority and acted on his own initiative, together with these eight states. In exercising the power to punish and reward, his commands did not issue from the royal court; in undertaking punitive campaigns, his troops were not directed by the Minister of War. Thus, the words “thereupon attacked Chu” censure his unauthorized action. Herein lies what is meant by rectifying names according to righteousness and teaching loyalty to all under Heaven.

…with Fangcheng as its city wall and the Han River as its moat, could not readily be subdued. Had Duke Huan set his heart on delighting in attacks and slaughter, and imposed his will upon Chu, what would there have been to commend? Fortunately, he drew the estranged into allegiance and conciliated those far away, summoning them to share in friendly relations [?]. Though his army was strong, he employed it with discipline and without brutality; once the enemy had submitted, he treated them with ritual courtesy and humility, without arrogance. This was like robbers submitting of their own accord, whereupon a gentleman does not pursue their past offenses. Did Huan not come close to commanding the army of a true king? Thus the entries “encamped at Xing,” “came to covenant with the army,” and “at Shaoling” recount his achievements. Herein lies what is meant by gladly helping others do good and showing the world an inducement to virtue.

Thus, in judging Duke Huan’s crimes, his accomplishments must nevertheless be recorded; in recording his accomplishments, his crimes must likewise not be concealed. Within a single manner of recording events, both rigor in establishing standards and generosity of heart are fully apparent. Yet in ritual propriety nothing is greater than distinctions of rank, and in distinctions of rank nothing is greater than titles. Chu usurped the title of king: its offense was grave. Why could Huan not rectify it? At that time, Qi had not requested the royal mandate, and its strength was insufficient to control Chu. It therefore merely secured a settlement and returned, taking this as a claim to renown. Otherwise, why overlook the greater offense and demand an accounting for the lesser? Alas! This is why the achievements of the Five Hegemons were of so low an order.

…his learning in adapting to change and benefiting the people can be gauged from this.
Examiner Yan, Right Admonisher, comments: “Refined and richly substantial, markedly different from other compositions.”
Examiner Kang, Expositor-in-waiting, comments: “The composition opens and closes, rises and falls, while verbal brilliance pours forth. An excellent work.”
The sage kings governed all under Heaven without going against its people. That popular customs differ in what suits them arises from circumstances. The sage kings simply followed these circumstances in governing; how could they force everyone to be alike? When the author of the Record of Rites discusses how the former kings settled people according to their capacities, he touches upon this point. His meaning is that government and instruction must be unified throughout the realm, whereas customs and what suits local conditions need not be uniform. In governing, the ancient sage kings likewise did no more than discern these distinctions.
Thus, since the people look to their ruler as their model, there must be something by which to lead them. The sovereign therefore establishes the supreme standard and guides those below through constant teachings. Looking to upright beginnings and goodness at the root [?], he gives weight to the established norms and rites as the basis for government. By dealing with each thing according to its own nature, instruction is thereby cultivated. Customs, however, arise from circumstances. Circumstances produce differences, and so customs throughout the realm are not uniform. I therefore follow them together with the people, accommodating them without altering them. It is not that I do not wish to alter them; they cannot be altered. Cultivating instruction means enlightening the people in accordance with their nature; accommodating customs also means adapting and shaping practices to realize their full benefits. Such indeed was the former kings’ excellence in government.
The people respond differently to moral transformation, so there must be something by which to bring them into unity. Thus one removes perversity and increases goodness, bringing them toward proper standards of conduct; one employs favor and authority, drawing them into a common moral transformation. 矣若夫宜也者率於其居者也居以方殊而天
下之宜各異矣吾則與民順之不拂其所欲也
非不欲拂也不可拂也夫政之齊也章程以敕
法而宜之順也又通變以宜民先王之善治又
如此夫政教以率天下而天下趨焉宜俗以便
天下而天下安焉此先王之治所以不可及也
雖然此非聖人意也勢也聖人豈不欲天下之
俗之宜皆歸於一哉勢則有所不可也故不順
人情者或以激天下之變而民俗之不可強者
===
亦聽之而已故曰后以裁成天地之道輔相天
地之宜以左右民后世變法之臣乃曰聖人苟
可以強國不法其故此拂人之性視聖人之治
何如耶
樂者敦和率神而從天禮者別宜居鬼而
從地故聖人作樂以應天制禮以配地

矣。若夫宜也者，率於其居者也。居以方殊，而天下之宜各異矣。吾則與民順之，不拂其所欲也。非不欲拂也，不可拂也。夫政之齊也，章程以敕法；而宜之順也，又通變以宜民。先王之善治又如此。夫政教以率天下，而天下趨焉；宜俗以便天下，而天下安焉。此先王之治所以不可及也。雖然，此非聖人意也，勢也。聖人豈不欲天下之俗之宜皆歸於一哉？勢則有所不可也。故不順人情者，或以激天下之變；而民俗之不可強者，亦聽之而已。故曰：「后以裁成天地之道，輔相天地之宜，以左右民。」后世變法之臣乃曰：「聖人苟可以強國，不法其故。」此拂人之性，視聖人之治何如耶？

樂者敦和，率神而從天；禮者別宜，居鬼而從地。故聖人作樂以應天，制禮以配地。禮樂明備，天地官矣。

translation_en:
…thus accomplished. As for what is locally fitting, it follows from where people dwell. Their dwellings differ by region, and so what is fitting differs throughout the realm. I therefore follow these circumstances together with the people, without opposing their wishes. It is not that I do not wish to oppose them, but that they cannot be opposed. To bring government into uniform order, regulations are established to put the laws in order; yet to follow what is locally fitting, adaptations are also made to suit the people. Such, too, was the good government of the former kings. Government and instruction guided all under Heaven, and all followed; accommodation to local conditions and customs served their convenience, and all were at peace. This is why the government of the former kings cannot be equaled. Yet this was not the sages’ intention: circumstances made it so. How could the sages not have wished that the customs and local practices of all under Heaven should be brought into unity? Circumstances, however, made some things impossible. Thus, failing to follow human feelings may provoke upheaval throughout the realm; customs that cannot be forcibly changed are simply left alone. Hence it is said: “The ruler shapes and brings to completion the Way of Heaven and Earth, assists what is fitting to Heaven and Earth, and thereby supports the people.” Yet ministers of later ages who altered the laws said: “If a sage can thereby strengthen the state, he does not model himself on its old ways.” This runs counter to human nature. How does it compare with the government of the sages?

Music deepens harmony, leads the spirits, and follows Heaven; ritual distinguishes what is fitting, settles the ghosts, and follows Earth. Thus the sages created music to respond to Heaven and instituted ritual to correspond to Earth. When ritual and music are manifest and complete, Heaven and Earth discharge their offices.

Comment by Associate Examiner Qiu, Instructor: Ritual and music, Heaven and Earth, ghosts and spirits—these are the true workings of creation…

記者論禮樂有合造化之妙，著聖人有叅造化之功。夫禮樂之用，與造化相爲流通者也。然非聖人之制作，又何以成叅賛之功哉？記者論禮樂而言此，若曰：造化妙禮樂於無形，禮樂闡造化於有象，使不明其合一之機，何以知其功用之大？今夫絪緼化醇，此造化自然之和，氣之伸也。而樂之爲用，則欣喜懽愛，有以厚其情之同，則氣之伸者以達，而顯仁之用行矣。高下散殊，此造化自然之序，氣之屈也。而禮之爲用，則莊敬恭順，有以辨其物之異，則氣之屈者以歛，而蔵用之機著矣。蓋和序之理，有以脗合造化之機，而屈伸之能，有以潛孚鬼神之妙。禮樂之爲用，蓋如此。故聖人者作，知自然之和，陽之所生
translation_en:
…Those who have not penetrated deeply into the Way can scarcely discuss this. This essay unfolds its subtle profundities as though walking on level ground. Moreover, its discussion of the principles of harmony and order, the capacities for contraction and expansion, the marvel of fully manifest and complete institutions, and the achievement of the sagely and spiritually perceptive in participating in and assisting cosmic transformation—all strike precisely at the essential points. Here one can discern the author's depth.
Examiner Yan, Right Mentor, comments: “The language and purport attain exceptional heights. Might this, too, be someone whose aspirations lie in rites and music?”
Examiner Kang, Expositor-in-waiting, comments: “The principles are clear and the language dignified [?]. This is someone who comprehends the foundations of rites and music.”
The author of the Record of Rites discusses how rites and music possess the marvel of accord with cosmic transformation, and makes clear the sages' achievement in participating in that transformation. The workings of rites and music and those of cosmic transformation flow through one another. Yet without the sages' establishment of institutions, how could the achievement of participating in and assisting transformation be accomplished? In discussing rites and music, the author of the Record says this as though to say: cosmic transformation gives wondrous operation to rites and music in the formless, while rites and music reveal cosmic transformation in perceptible forms. Unless one understands the workings of their unity, how can one know the greatness of their efficacy?
Now, the intermingling of cosmic forces and their transformation into a rich fullness constitute the spontaneous harmony of cosmic transformation: the expansion of vital energy. Music, in its workings, brings joy, delight, affection, and love, thereby deepening the feelings people share. Thus expanding vital energy finds expression, and its function of manifesting benevolence comes into operation. The dispersion and differentiation of high and low constitute the spontaneous order of cosmic transformation: the contraction of vital energy. Rites, in their workings, bring solemnity, respect, reverence, and compliance, thereby distinguishing differences among things. Thus contracting vital energy is gathered in, and the workings by which efficacy is stored become apparent.
The principles of harmony and order accord with the workings of cosmic transformation, while the capacities for contraction and expansion secretly correspond to the wonders of ghosts and spirits. Such are the workings of rites and music. Thus, when the sage arises, he recognizes that spontaneous harmony is what yang generates…

至誠贊天地之化育
translation_en:
…and so creates music in response to it, organizing it through the five tones and giving it expression through the six pitch standards, thereby making manifest the work of bringing things into being and harmonizing with it. Knowing that the order of nature is accomplished by yin, the sage establishes ritual to match it, distinguishing ranks and dignities and displaying them through ceremonial objects and adornments, thereby establishing the work of bringing things to completion and becoming one with it. Thus these institutions attain the utmost refinement in clarity and completeness, preserving the Way of regulating and assisting the processes of nature. The sage, with spiritlike understanding, can participate in and assist these processes, while the functions of birth, growth, harvest, and storage are each established. This is what is meant by: “When ritual and music are clear and complete, Heaven and Earth fulfill their offices.” Indeed, Heaven and Earth must attain their proper positions through ritual and music!

At the outset, the harmony and order of Heaven and Earth provide the sage with a model to follow; afterward, the sage’s ritual and music participate in and assist Heaven and Earth. Such is the greatness of the efficacy of ritual and music! This is the marvel of equilibrium and harmony, through which Heaven and Earth take their proper positions and all things are nourished; it is the achievement of utmost sincerity, through which one fully realizes one’s nature. Who but the sage could participate in this? Hence it is said: “Only after understanding Heaven and Earth can one institute ritual and music.” As for such later examples as Shusun’s ritual rehearsed with bundles of reeds, or the music of Lady Fangshan [?], to speak in their case of Heaven and Earth fulfilling their offices would surely be superficial! Ah! A thousand years later, should an enlightened king arise, fortunately the words recording ritual still remain.

Second Session

Discourse

Through Utmost Sincerity, Assisting the Transforming and Nourishing Work of Heaven and Earth

理完具於吾身終而以吾身之理叅贊乎天地
亦惟代天而成其能焉耳而非有所加也夫人

translation_en:
…and assist where their workings fall short. How could this be spoken of lightly? At the outset, the principles of Heaven and Earth are fully present within oneself; ultimately, through the principles within oneself, one participates in and assists Heaven and Earth. This is merely to act on Heaven’s behalf and bring its capacities to fulfillment, not to add anything to them. Who, indeed, first brought human beings and other things into existence? The Book of Changes says: “Great is Qian’s primal power: the myriad things draw upon it for their beginnings. Utmost is Kun’s primal power: the myriad things draw upon it for their birth.” Thus, the birth of human beings and other things is rooted in Heaven and Earth. Master Zhou says: “Great is Qian’s primal power: the myriad things draw upon it for their beginnings. This is the source of sincerity. The Way of Qian changes and transforms, and each thing attains its proper nature and allotted endowment. Thereby sincerity is established.” Sincerity, then, is also the foundation upon which Heaven and Earth generate human beings and other things. If we examine the time before human beings and other things have come into existence, material force (qi) is contained within principle (li), and the foundation of transformation and nurture is established. If we examine the time after they have come into existence, principle operates within material force, and the functioning of transformation and nurture proceeds. This is one numinous agency with two modes of transformation. It would thus seem that the transformative and nurturing work of Heaven and Earth, enduring through time and bringing things to completion, has no need of the sage.

Yet yin and yang differ in their material forces; the hard and the soft differ in their constitutions; dullness and intelligence, strength and weakness, differ in their endowments; and transformation through material force and transformation through physical form vary in countless ways. Consequently, some people fail to accord with their nature, and some things fail to fulfill their lives. Thus, the transformative and nurturing work of Heaven and Earth reaches some things but falls short of others. Unless a sage emerges to assist where it falls short and bring its capacities to fulfillment, the work of creation and transformation might all but cease. If that work ceased, to whom could the sage shift his responsibility? Moreover, at birth the sage receives the finest of the finest essence. His virtue is formed by Heaven; his sageliness…

text:
則天縱也其感則誠之通也其寂則誠之復也
一理流通渾然無間故其道之隆也象天其一
而不遷也象地其繼明以照也象日月其變動
不居也象風雨其行有序而不愆于常足以配

之天下之物無不準焉自人物之性而達之於

translation_en:
…is Heaven-bestowed. His responsiveness is sincerity flowing outward; his stillness is sincerity returning to itself. The single principle circulates throughout, an undivided whole without interruption. Thus his Way resembles Heaven in its loftiness, Earth in its unity and constancy, the sun and moon in its continuing illumination, and wind and rain in its ceaseless transformations. Its operation is orderly and never departs from the constant pattern, sufficient to match the four seasons. Its wondrous changes are unfathomable; issuing forth and withdrawing, benefiting all through its operation and working unceasingly, it is sufficient to resemble the spirits. Indeed, he becomes one with the creative transformations of the cosmos. Wherever his achievements extend, they and Heaven and Earth illuminate one another. Truly, none but one of utmost sincerity can participate in this.

Thus, when I extend the nature of my own person to all people under Heaven, it accords with them all; when I extend our human nature to all things under Heaven, it accords with them all; and when I extend the nature of people and things to Heaven and Earth, it accords with them both. Preserved within, it constitutes the substance of benevolence, righteousness, centrality, and correctness. Spread abroad, it functions as rites, music, punishments, and government. Applied in practice, it establishes what is fitting in demeanor, bearing, reverence, and distinctions. Wielded as authority, it deliberates on rites, establishes institutions and measures, and examines written forms. Put into operation, it brings to completeness the universally binding ways, the universally applicable virtues, and the nine guiding principles of government. Nothing is understood without clarity; nothing is handled without fittingness.

He governs people according to their humanity and assigns things their due according to their nature. He responds to change without weariness and brings each thing to fulfillment in all its particularities, overlooking none. Thus all who wear caps and girdles, and every kind of living being, receive auspicious blessings. His profound beneficence flows abundantly, bringing well-being within and beyond the realm. The common people enjoy supreme harmony, and the myriad states are all at peace. Mountains, rivers, and spirits are all in accord; every tiny creature that flies, crawls, or breathes follows its proper course. Heaven thereby attains clarity, and Earth tranquility. It comes not from striving to embrace and encompass everything, or from laboriously pondering how to form a triad with Heaven and Earth: it is sincerity alone. Through sincerity, transformation is made abundant; through transformation, spiritual efficacy is fully realized; through spiritual efficacy, benefit is fully realized. The principles of Heaven, Earth, and the myriad things are all present in my own person; no principle is found missing from it. The principles within my person extend throughout Heaven, Earth, and the myriad things; no thing under Heaven is found left out. Following their course without error, operating without exhaustion—the means by which this fulfillment and assistance are achieved are unknown to Heaven and Earth, unknown to the myriad things, and unknown even to the sage himself.

The affairs of successive reigns are collected, their brilliance illuminating generations to come. We, your servants, in profound awe and fear, bow our heads to the ground and kowtow, submitting these words.
We humbly reflect that, from antiquity, emperors and kings governing the world have invariably placed established standards first. Only by fully establishing institutions and fulfilling human relationships could they assemble around, and conform to, the supreme standard. Fuxi and Xuanyuan opened the world to human use, and laws and institutions first arose; Yao and Shun ruled in accordance with Heaven, and their canons and counsels were set forth. When Xia and Shang received the transferred Mandate, the additions and omissions made by their two kings could be known; when Wen and Wu renewed the royal radiance, the regulations of their dynasty became especially complete. Qin and Han esteemed the office charged with institutional precedents; Tang and Song valued compilations of institutional essentials. All recorded the achievements of government in their own times, thereby transmitting established rules to succeeding generations.
Heaven inaugurated our sagely dynasty, whose destined rule coincided with an age of auspicious enlightenment. Emperor Gao laid grand plans for its foundation; the successive sage emperors advanced the achievements of their inheritance. The cardinal bonds, constant virtues, rites, and music renewed the aspect of the Chinese realm over a hundred years; institutions, statutes, and regulations made its enlightened government shine through the ages. For written records and worthy testimony to provide adequate verification, the established models had to remain available. 問，知紀載之失真者未免，而事例之續定者當增。廼渙宸裁，重加纂輯。顧譔述未就，尚停閣之多年，恐久遠易忘，何傳信於來世？頃因申請，復命增脩，開局分曹，循先朝之故事；列官供職，萃秘閣之儒臣；發金匱石室之藏，徵兩京百司之籍。蓋自弘治壬戌以至嘉靖戊子，已輯而未成；自己丑之春以至戊申之冬，尚缺而未載。分條附例，綱舉而目則隨；舉要刪繁，文約而事已備。校閱集諸曹之彥，編摩效數歲之勞。既因舊以為新，亦刋訛而訂誤。中間四十七載之因革損益，各比類以相從；國家百八十年之經制紀綱，一開卷而易見。曰用人，曰立政，成法具在目前；曰酌古，曰準今，治道可運掌上。是皆聖謨之默運，故大典之聿成也。

…inquiry, which revealed that inaccuracies in the records had not been entirely avoided, and that subsequently established precedents ought to be added. An imperial decision was thereupon promulgated, ordering the compilation to be undertaken anew. Yet the work remained unfinished and lay suspended for many years. Fearing that matters would readily be forgotten with the passage of time, how could we transmit a trustworthy account to future generations? Recently, in response to a petition, another command was issued to expand and revise the work. A compilation office was opened and its work divided among sections, following the precedents of earlier reigns. Officials were appointed to their duties, bringing together the scholarly officials of the imperial library. The holdings of the golden chests and stone chambers were opened, and records were requisitioned from the many offices of the two capitals.
For the period from the renxu year of Hongzhi to the wuzi year of Jiajing, material had already been compiled but the work remained incomplete; for the period from the spring of the jichou year to the winter of the wushen year, material was still missing and had not been recorded. Topics were distinguished and precedents appended: once the main framework was set out, the particulars followed. Essentials were selected and excessive detail removed, making the text concise while keeping its coverage complete. Outstanding men from the various offices were assembled to review the text, and several years of labor were devoted to its compilation. Drawing upon the old, we produced the new, while also removing inaccuracies and correcting errors. The continuities and changes, reductions and additions, of these forty-seven years were each grouped with matters of the same kind. The established institutions and governing principles of the dynasty’s one hundred and eighty years could thus be readily seen as soon as one opened the book. Whether employing men or establishing government, the settled rules lie fully before one’s eyes; whether weighing antiquity or taking the present as a standard, the methods of governing can be handled as readily as something in the palm of one’s hand. All this results from the unseen working of Your Majesty’s sagacious designs; hence this great compendium has at last been completed.
We, your servants, have long held office in the Hanlin Academy, yet are ashamed that our learning offers scarcely a single useful insight. Undeservedly entrusted with editorial responsibility in the Historiography Office, we are ashamed that our understanding falls short of the historian’s three strengths. …the fundamental institutions of the state; in truth, we have merely reverently followed Your Majesty’s decisions. In recording years and events, we can scarcely escape criticism for shallowness; in taking up our brushes and recording words, how could we avoid errors of omission? May this work reach Your Majesty’s august gaze, and may you condescend to examine it during the second watch of the night. May your imperial composition, a celestial blossom, be inscribed by your own hand upon its opening pages; may its grand regulations and excellent models be disseminated forever throughout the realm.
We humbly wish that your consummate governance may be free from troubles, and that your provision for your descendants may endure for ten thousand generations; that great peace may have its manifest signs, and that your exalted fame may stand alone above that of the hundred kings. May qilin appear and phoenixes roam, their numinous presence answering the auspicious signs of your sagely rule; may sacred tortoises appear and stars gather in the Kui mansion, gloriously manifesting literary culture. Five Policy Questions
First Question

Comment by Associate Examiner Luo, District Magistrate:
Our imperial ancestors and the present Emperor have grounded their great transforming influence in sagely virtue. Yet they have also selected and appointed Confucian officials to assist in governance. Their guiding principle accords entirely with the eagerness of Yao and Shun to draw worthy men close. This policy essay alone sets forth their merits clearly and comprehensively. Accept it.

Comment by Associate Examiner Yang, Prefectural Judge:
The sagely progenitor and divine ancestor [神宗, Shenzong?] established the dynasty’s grand foundations, employing worthy men to provide enlightened counsel and emulating the admirable models of the ancient emperors and kings. Our present Emperor has worthily continued their glorious achievements, drawing worthy men close and striving for good government. Truly, he has thereby manifested the brilliant radiance of the two sages—something of which later students cannot glimpse even one ten-thousandth. This composition expounds everything fully; its author is indeed a man of outstanding talent.

…the two ancestral emperors. You have expounded and extolled this with utmost clarity and completeness. Surely you have gained something from being nurtured by the sage influence and now wish to put it to use in service?

Comment by Examiner Kang, Expositor: In employing worthy men to achieve good government, our ancestral emperors and our present sovereign illuminate one another across successive reigns. You have answered each point fully and in detail. Surely you are one who has benefited most deeply from the sage influence?

When emperors establish the enterprise of a rising dynasty, they must draw upon eminent scholars to accomplish their work; to bring about an age of Great Peace, they must likewise rely upon outstanding worthies to carry it through together. If the right men are absent at the founding, plans for bringing peace and succor to the realm will be inadequate; if they are absent in preserving the dynasty, the practice of enlightening and nourishing the ruler’s mind will fall into neglect. It is then difficult to accomplish a great enterprise and achieve flourishing government. Yet worthy and talented men, born in response to destiny and emerging when the time calls, have never been few. Only when ruler and ministers concentrate their energies and unite their minds, each enhancing the other’s brilliance, can their encounter, like that of wind and clouds, suffice to accomplish the work of assisting a ruler to fulfill Heaven’s mandate. Their devoted deliberation and reflection can likewise suffice to bring about the enterprise of Great Peace. Thus our Emperor Gao, Taizu, recruited heroes in the unsettled days of the founding, and Emperor Wen, Chengzu, sought wise men far and wide when pursuing good government. This enabled them to surpass other emperors and inaugurate boundless blessings for our Ming for countless ages. Could one say that this was not their foundation? Permit me respectfully to set it forth.

Shun had his five ministers, and King Wu his ten ministers who brought order; their government through nonaction and the blessings of ruling with folded hands were unequalled throughout antiquity [?]. The song celebrating an enlightened ruler and worthy ministers joyfully rising to their tasks, and the image of the phoenix and the parasol tree, are why their achievements remain illustrious to this day. We reverently reflect that our Taizu responded to Heaven and accorded with the people, received the great mandate, and established achievements unprecedented in all antiquity. 無雙文章第一則有若陶安文武全才廉
正厲俗則有若章溢奉使死節日月爭光
則有若王禕守土治民保城血戰則有若
葉琛許瑗其餘樹勳立業有不能盡舉者
矣當時肇造家邦混一六合雖曰開國元
勳六王之功而疑丞夾輔諸臣之力其可
少哉
===
成祖嗣登寶位寤寐賢良自癸未開
文淵閣以處文學侍從之臣時則以侍讀召
入者解縉也以修撰召入者胡廣也以編
脩召入者楊榮也楊士奇也以檢討召入
者金幼孜也黃淮也胡儼也此皆不介而
punctuated:
言而情已密。或徵以書幣，或從容賜坐，或稱曰先生，或留叅幕府，或賜書奨諭，推心置腹，如手足腹心，不言自喻。故一時之臣感激思奮，宣力陳猷，則有可言者矣。運籌决勝，燭物炳幾，為時王佐者，劉基也；闢邪翼正，潤色皇猷，為世儒宗者，宋濂也；謀畧無雙，文章第一，則有若陶安；文武全才，亷正勵俗，則有若章溢；奉使死節，日月爭光，則有若王禕；守土治民，保城血戰，則有若葉琛、許瑗。其餘樹勲立業，有不能盡舉者矣。當時肇造家邦，混一六合，雖曰開國元勲六王之功，而疑丞夾輔諸臣之力，其可少哉？
成祖嗣登寶位，寤寐賢良，自癸未開文淵閣，以處文學侍從之臣。時則以侍讀召入者，解縉也；以修撰召入者，胡廣也；以編脩召入者，楊榮也、楊士竒也；以檢討召入者，金幼孜也、黄淮也、胡儼也。此皆不介而
translation_en:
…before words were spoken, their feelings were already close. Some he summoned with letters and gifts; some he graciously invited to sit; some he addressed as “Master”; some he retained on his military staff; and some he encouraged and instructed through letters. He opened his heart to them and trusted them completely, treating them as his own limbs and innermost confidants; understanding required no words. Thus the ministers of that time, moved by his favor and eager to exert themselves, rendered service and offered counsel in ways worthy of recounting. Liu Ji devised strategies that secured victory, discerned affairs and the first signs of change, and served as an adviser fit to assist a true king. Song Lian opposed heterodoxy, upheld orthodoxy, gave literary expression to imperial plans, and became a leading Confucian scholar of his age. For unrivaled strategy and writings of the highest order, there was Tao An. For comprehensive civil and military abilities, and integrity and uprightness that encouraged good customs, there was Zhang Yi. For dying in fidelity to his duty while on an embassy, with a glory rivaling the sun and moon, there was Wang Yi. For defending territory, governing the people, and fighting bloody battles to hold their cities, there were Ye Chen and Xu Yuan. The others who established achievements and rendered distinguished service cannot all be enumerated. In founding the dynasty and unifying all under Heaven, the achievement may be attributed to the six princes, the foremost founding heroes; yet could the contributions of the ministers who counseled and assisted the sovereign have been dispensed with?
Chengzu succeeded to the imperial throne and longed for worthy men, waking and sleeping. In the gu未 year [1403], he opened the Wenyuan Pavilion to accommodate literary officials serving in attendance. Xie Jin was summoned to enter as Reader-in-waiting; Hu Guang as Senior Compiler; Yang Rong and Yang Shiqi as Junior Compilers; and Jin Youzi, Huang Huai, and Hu Yan as Examining Editors. All these, without an intermediary, …

title: 嘉靖二十八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
自孚不謀而自合或賜大學衍義或賜金
織縷衣或扆前顧問漏下十數刻乃退或
臨幸私宅或賜繩愆糾繆圖書情意浹洽
如家人父子相視無間故一時之臣感恩
圖報沃心煕載則有可言者矣弼亮
東宮保全趙邸中流砥柱者文貞也通才敏
識文武兼資全節完名者文敏也恪勤始
終金温玉粹則有若文靖定策安邦省愆
翼翼則有若文簡清慎恭勤終始一節則
===
有若文穆諫沮交阯力抗權倖則有若解
縉出教成均師範嚴肅則有若胡儼其餘
忠謀遠畧有不能盡舉者矣當時中外肅
清四夷賓服雖奉天靖難武臣有功而翼
輔賛襄諸臣之力其可少哉是則創之於
前收儒碩以成功者
聖祖也繼之於後任輔弼以致治者
成祖也此其
訏謨定於逸軌

punctuated: 自孚，不謀而自合。或賜《大學衍義》，或賜金織縷衣，或扆前顧問，漏下十數刻乃退，或臨幸私宅，或賜「繩愆糾繆」圖書。情意浹洽，如家人父子，相視無間。故一時之臣感恩圖報，沃心煕載，則有可言者矣。弼亮東宮，保全趙邸，中流砥柱者，文貞也；通才敏識，文武兼資，全節完名者，文敏也；恪勤始終，金温玉粹，則有若文靖；定策安邦，省愆翼翼，則有若文簡；清慎恭勤，終始一節，則有若文穆；諫沮交阯，力抗權倖，則有若解縉；出教成均，師範嚴肅，則有若胡儼。其餘忠謀遠畧，有不能盡舉者矣。當時中外肅清，四夷賓服，雖奉天靖難武臣有功，而翼輔賛襄諸臣之力，其可少哉？是則創之於前，收儒碩以成功者，聖祖也；繼之於後，任輔弼以致治者，成祖也。此其訏謨定於逸軌
translation_en:
…of themselves won his trust, and without prior consultation found themselves in accord. Sometimes he bestowed the Extended Meaning of the Great Learning (Daxue yanyi); sometimes, garments woven with gold thread. Sometimes he consulted them before the imperial screen, and they withdrew only after ten or more quarter-hours had passed on the water clock. Sometimes he visited their private residences, or bestowed seals bearing the words “Correct faults and rectify errors.” Their feelings were harmonious and intimate, like those of fathers and sons within a family, with no estrangement between them. Thus the ministers of that time, grateful for his favor and intent on repaying it, enlightened the sovereign’s mind and brought distinction to their duties; their achievements deserve to be recounted.

Wenzhen assisted and guided the heir apparent, preserved the Prince of Zhao’s household, and stood firm like a pillar amid the current. Wenmin possessed comprehensive talents and keen discernment, combined civil and military abilities, and preserved his integrity and reputation intact. For conscientious diligence from beginning to end, with the warmth of gold and purity of jade, there was Wenjing. For settling great questions of state and securing the realm, while vigilantly examining his own faults, there was Wenjian. For purity, circumspection, reverence, and diligence, maintaining consistent integrity throughout, there was Wenmu. For remonstrating against the Jiaozhi undertaking and stoutly resisting powerful imperial favorites, there was Xie Jin. For going out to teach at the Directorate of Education and serving as a strict and dignified exemplar to students, there was Hu Yan. The loyal counsels and far-reaching strategies of the others cannot all be enumerated.

At that time, order prevailed within and beyond the court, and the peoples of the four quarters submitted. Although military officials had rendered service in obeying Heaven and quelling the troubles, could the contributions of the ministers who supported and assisted the ruler have been dispensed with? Thus it was Shengzu, the Sagely Progenitor, who established the foundation and recruited eminent Confucian scholars to accomplish the enterprise; it was Chengzu who succeeded him and entrusted assisting ministers with bringing about good government. In this, his grand plans were established upon lofty precedents [?]…

title: 嘉靖二十八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
厭心困於今圖
淵猷集於眾思
熈烈裒之忠益蓋先後一者也故豪彥尋聲
而響臻志士希光而景騖治理之隆不可
尚已他如虎觀石渠之論覈集賢麗正之
招延崇政邇英之講說其跡若勤而其功
未究烏可以擬其萬一哉
列聖相承率用是道
重熈累洽百有餘年逮我
===
皇上龍興益隆繼述
敬一傳心
禮樂飾治
中興之烈既振古有光矣然猶不自滿假
虛懷圖治
側席求賢往歲
親御
文華選庶吉士若干人儲養翰林頒之筆札
給以酒飯間歲舉行宛然禮賢館之遺意

punctuated: 厭心困於今圖，淵猷集於眾思，熈烈裒之忠益，蓋先後一者也。故豪彥尋聲而響臻，志士希光而景騖，治理之隆不可尚已。他如虎觀、石渠之論覈，集賢、麗正之招延，崇政、邇英之講說，其跡若勤，而其功未究，烏可以擬其萬一哉！列聖相承，率用是道，重熈累洽百有餘年。逮我皇上龍興，益隆繼述，敬一傳心，禮樂飾治，中興之烈既振古有光矣。然猶不自滿假，虛懷圖治，側席求賢。往歲親御文華，選庶吉士若干人，儲養翰林，頒之筆札，給以酒飯，間歲舉行，宛然禮賢館之遺意
translation_en:
…their minds were burdened by present plans [?]; their profound designs drew upon the thoughts of many, and their glorious achievements gathered strength from loyal contributions. In this, predecessor and successor were indeed at one. Thus outstanding men followed their call and arrived like answering echoes; men of resolve aspired to their radiance and hastened toward it like shadows. The excellence of their government could not be surpassed. As for the discussions and examinations at Huguan and Shiqu, the recruitment of scholars at Jixian and Lizheng, and the lectures at Chongzheng and Erying, these activities may have appeared diligent, yet their results were never fully realized. How could they compare with even a ten-thousandth part of these achievements!

The successive sage emperors all followed this course, accumulating brilliance and sustaining harmonious rule for more than a hundred years. When our present emperor rose like a dragon, he further magnified the work of carrying on his predecessors’ achievements. Through reverence for the One, he transmitted their understanding; through rites and music, he adorned his government. The achievements of his restoration have already brought lustre to the ages. Yet he remains free of complacency, humbly planning good government and leaving a place beside him as he seeks worthy men.

In a previous year, he personally visited Wenhua Hall and selected a number of Hanlin bachelors, nurturing them in the Hanlin Academy as a reserve of talent. He bestowed brushes and writing materials upon them and provided them with wine and meals. Held in alternate years, this practice vividly recalls the spirit of the Lixian Hall, the Hall for Honoring Worthy Men…

title: 嘉靖二十八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
也而
內閣重地必
簡用文學侍從之臣以代
言備問不計新故崇卑隆以股肱心膂之托
藹然
文淵閣之故事也
神謨睿慮蓋與
二祖之見異世同符故自
臨御以来二十八年
===
道化隆洽
玄澤汪濊得人之治有光前古而一時儒臣
遘泰逢陽爭自磨濯所以弼成萬世無疆
之休者先後輝映此豈草莽之臣所能盡
述哉書曰股肱惟人良臣惟聖敢以是爲
聖天子頌詩曰濟濟多士文王以寧敢以是爲
諸臣頌謹對
第二問

臨御以來二十八年
===
道化隆洽
玄澤汪濊得人之治有光前古而一時儒臣
遭泰逢陽爭自磨濯所以缵成萬世無疆
之休者先後輝映此豈草莽之臣所能盡
述哉書曰股肱惟人良臣惟聖敢以是爲
聖天子頌詩曰濟濟多士文王以寧敢以是爲
諸臣頌謹對
第二問
punctuated:
也。而內閣重地，必簡用文學侍從之臣，以代言備問，不計新故崇卑，隆以股肱心膂之托，藹然文淵閣之故事也。神謨睿慮，蓋與二祖之見異世同符。故自臨御以来二十八年，道化隆洽，玄澤汪濊，得人之治有光前古。而一時儒臣遘泰逢陽，爭自磨濯，所以弼成萬世無疆之休者，先後輝映。此豈草莽之臣所能盡述哉？書曰：「股肱惟人，良臣惟聖。」敢以是爲聖天子頌。詩曰：「濟濟多士，文王以寧。」敢以是爲諸臣頌。謹對。

第二問
translation_en:
…indeed. For the Grand Secretariat, a place of weighty responsibility, Your Majesty invariably selects literary attendants to speak on your behalf and stand ready to answer your inquiries. Without regard to length of service or high or low rank, you honor them with the trust placed in your limbs and innermost counselors. Here the precedents of the Wenyuan Pavilion are abundantly manifest. Your divine plans and sagacious deliberations accord with the vision of the two ancestral emperors, though their ages differ. Thus, throughout the twenty-eight years since you ascended the throne, moral transformation has flourished and spread, and your profound beneficence has flowed in abundance. Your government, through securing worthy men, has lent luster surpassing antiquity. The Confucian ministers of this age, encountering prosperity and favor, have vied in polishing and purifying themselves. Their contributions toward bringing boundless blessings to fruition for ten thousand generations shine forth in succession. How could a servant living among the common people fully recount them?

The Book of Documents says: “Arms and legs make the person; good ministers make the sage.” I venture to offer these words in praise of the sagely Son of Heaven. The Book of Odes says: “Numerous were the worthy men; through them King Wen enjoyed peace.” I venture to offer these words in praise of the ministers. Respectfully submitted in reply.

Second Question

title: 嘉靖二十八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
同考試官教諭朱批文章士習所繫固不可以
雕蟲小技目之也近日士子崇尚竒詭摹倣成風於
國初渾厚之氣漸以漓薄主司有深憂焉子獨能振起流俗破摸擬剽畧之藩籬
而一歸之正可以占子學之富識之明矣録之以式豈徒文焉已哉
考試官右贊善閻批此策歷指諸家文體醇駁而斷
以已意且詞氣奔放若驥騁康莊要其歸弗畔於理亦可謂篤
文矣
考試官侍講康批論文一策正欲觀士子稽古之
學子能條荅詳明評隲精確末復歸之於心悟盖稽古而有
===
得者録之
君子之為文非得已也將以闡性命之原
昭彜倫之懿理性情之正著理亂之經嚴
義利之辨而非有意而為之也後世諸子
非不崇志藝林揚芳詞圃出入四部頡頏
九經然學步效顰鬭靡逞巧或追風以入
麗或沿波以遡竒所謂有之靡所益無之
靡所闋者也尚奚以文為哉執事策諸生
以漢魏以來諸子之著述為問豈非厭摸

君子之為文非得已也將以闡性命之原
昭彞倫之懿理性情之正著理亂之經嚴

麗或沿波以遡竒所謂有之靡所益無之
靡所闕者也尚奚以文為哉執事策諸生
以漢魏以來諸子之著述為問豈非厭模
punctuated:
同考試官教諭朱批：文章，士習所繫，固不可以雕蟲小技目之也。近日士子崇尚竒詭，摹倣成風，於國初渾厚之氣漸以漓薄，主司有深憂焉。子獨能振起流俗，破摸擬剽畧之藩籬，而一歸之正，可以占子學之富、識之明矣。録之以式，豈徒文焉已哉！

考試官右贊善閻批：此策歷指諸家文體醇駁，而斷以已意，且詞氣奔放，若驥騁康莊。要其歸，弗畔於理，亦可謂篤文矣。

考試官侍講康批：論文一策，正欲觀士子稽古之學。子能條荅詳明，評隲精確，末復歸之於心悟，盖稽古而有得者。録之。

君子之為文，非得已也，將以闡性命之原，昭彜倫之懿，理性情之正，著理亂之經，嚴義利之辨，而非有意而為之也。後世諸子，非不崇志藝林，揚芳詞圃，出入四部，頡頏九經；然學步效顰，鬭靡逞巧，或追風以入麗，或沿波以遡竒，所謂有之靡所益，無之靡所闋者也。尚奚以文為哉！執事策諸生，以漢魏以來諸子之著述為問，豈非厭摸
translation_en:
Comment by Associate Examiner Zhu, Instructor: Literary composition shapes the habits of scholars and certainly cannot be regarded as a petty skill of carving insects. Recently, candidates have prized the strange and bizarre, and imitation has become fashionable. The substantial, generous spirit of the dynasty’s founding has gradually grown thin and insubstantial, causing the examiners deep concern. You alone can rouse those caught in prevailing fashions, break through the barriers of imitation and plagiarism, and return entirely to what is correct. This reveals the breadth of your learning and the clarity of your discernment. We select this as a model: could our purpose concern literary composition alone?

Comment by Examiner Yan, Right Admonisher: This policy essay identifies in turn the purity and admixture in the literary styles of the various writers and judges them according to the author’s own views. Its language and spirit are free and vigorous, like a thoroughbred galloping down a broad highway. In its ultimate import, it does not depart from principle. It may indeed be called substantial writing.

Comment by Examiner Kang, Expositor-in-waiting: This policy question on literary composition was intended precisely to examine candidates’ learning through the study of antiquity. Your answers proceed point by point, clearly and fully, and your assessments are precise. At the end, you return to understanding gained in one’s own mind. You are evidently someone who has studied antiquity and gained insight from it. Selected.

When the gentleman writes, he does so because he cannot do otherwise. His purpose is to elucidate the origins of human nature and Heaven’s mandate, illuminate the beauty of the enduring human relationships, set human nature and feelings in their proper order, make manifest the guiding principles of order and disorder, and distinguish rigorously between righteousness and profit. He does not write merely with the deliberate intention of producing a composition. The writers of later ages certainly set their ambitions high in the forest of letters, spread their fragrance in the garden of language, ranged through the Four Divisions of literature, and vied with the Nine Classics. Yet they copied others’ steps and imitated others’ frowns, competed in extravagance and displayed their ingenuity. Some chased the wind to attain ornate beauty; others followed the waves upstream in pursuit of novelty. These are what are described as works whose presence adds nothing and whose absence leaves nothing lacking. What use, then, is such writing? You, honored examiners, have tested us candidates with a question about the writings of authors since the Han and Wei dynasties. Is this not because you have grown weary of imitation …

title: 嘉靖二十八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
擬之爲工而欲崇明聖之述作懲剽畧之
爲僭而欲回同文之盛治甚大惠也愚也
嘗聞諸先哲之論文也曰風行水上天下
之至文也夫水之爲體澄然清而已矣淵
然靜而已矣風一過之則紆餘委蛇蜿蜒
淪連疾者如馳徐者如緬蹙者如鱗躍者
如鯉其繁如榖其亂如霧而天下之極觀
備矣人而能知風行水上之文斯可以論
文矣昔者夫子於易吾見其思焉而得之
===
也於詩書吾見其諷焉而得之也於春秋
吾見其感焉而得之者也於論語吾見其
觸焉而得之者也故其讀易也如未嘗有
書其讀詩也如未嘗有易其讀論語也如
未嘗有春秋各以道顯而體不相沿於易
而闡性命之原也於書而昭彛倫之懿也
於詩而理性情之正也於春秋而著理亂
之經也於論語而嚴義利之辨也矢口爲
經措詞爲訓經緯天地貫徹古今遐哉邈

昔者夫子於《易》，吾見其思焉而得之也；於《詩》《書》，吾見其諷焉而得之也；於《春秋》，吾見其感焉而得之者也；於《論語》，吾見其觸焉而得之者也。故其讀《易》也，如未嘗有《書》；其讀《詩》也，如未嘗有《易》；其讀《論語》也，如未嘗有《春秋》。各以道顯，而體不相沿。於《易》而闡性命之原也，於《書》而昭彛倫之懿也，於《詩》而理性情之正也，於《春秋》而著理亂之經也，於《論語》而嚴義利之辨也。矢口爲經，措詞爲訓，經緯天地，貫徹古今，遐哉邈
translation_en:
…taking imitation as craftsmanship, and wishing to exalt the writings of enlightened sages; condemning plagiarism as usurpation, and wishing to restore the flourishing governance of a realm united in its written culture—is this not a very great kindness? I, in my ignorance, have heard earlier worthies discuss writing in these terms: “Wind moving over water is the finest pattern under Heaven.” Water in its essential state is simply limpid and clear, deep and still. Once the wind passes over it, however, it twists and meanders, winds and ripples continuously. Its swift movements seem to gallop; its slow ones seem to stretch into the distance [?]; its compressed ripples resemble scales, its leaping waves carp. Its profusion resembles the paper-mulberry tree [?], its disordered movement mist: all the world's most magnificent sights are present there. Only someone who understands the patterns of wind moving over water can discuss literary composition.
In the Master's engagement with the Book of Changes, I see what he attained through reflection; in the Book of Odes and the Book of Documents, what he attained through recitation; in the Spring and Autumn Annals, what he attained through being moved by events; and in the Analects, what he attained through encounters with particular circumstances. Thus, when reading the Changes, it is as though the Documents had never existed; when reading the Odes, as though the Changes had never existed; and when reading the Analects, as though the Spring and Autumn Annals had never existed. Each makes the Way manifest, yet their forms do not follow one another. The Changes elucidates the source of human nature and destiny; the Documents illuminates the beauty of the enduring human relationships; the Odes orders human nature and feelings in their proper condition; the Spring and Autumn Annals makes clear the principles of order and disorder; and the Analects draws a strict distinction between righteousness and profit. What issued from his mouth became canonical teaching; the words he set down became instruction. They give structure to Heaven and Earth and run through past and present. How far-reaching, how boundless …

title: 嘉靖二十八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
乎蔑以尚矣自崇論閎議之風熾而昔人
之質漓自摸擬僭竊之習興而斯文之致
乖故太史公曰學者載籍極博猶考信於
六藝然秦漢以下之文視之六藝何如耶
是故楊雄作法言而言未必可法王通作
中說而說未必得中太玄準易也君子有
吳楚僭王之譏續經擬經也君子有六經
奴婢之誚二子且然况其下者乎觀班固
藝文志所載易有十三家書有九家詩有
===
六家禮有十三家春秋二十三家論語十
二家凡六藝一百三家各引一端崇其所
善或互相闡明或私自譔述非不爛然於
文墨之場也然而紀載雖多而實理益晦
擬議雖勤而道法不存其於六經論語之
旨既未必有所發明視之王楊之作又瞠
乎其後矣又何必盡舉而述之哉夫子雲
之作高者出蒼天深者入黄泉雖云貴知
我者希而不免覆醬瓿之誚惟仲淹之作

translation_en:
…indeed! Nothing could surpass them. Once the fashion for lofty arguments and grand discussions flourished, the substance of the ancients was diluted; once the practice of imitation and presumptuous appropriation arose, the purport of this literary tradition went astray. Thus the Grand Historian said: “Scholars have an immense range of written records, yet still test their reliability against the Six Arts.” But how does the writing of the Qin and Han and later ages compare with the Six Arts?

Thus Yang Xiong composed Model Sayings (Fayan), yet his sayings were not necessarily worthy of being taken as models; Wang Tong composed Discussions of the Mean (Zhongshuo), yet his discussions did not necessarily attain the mean. The Supreme Mystery (Taixuan) took the Book of Changes as its standard, but gentlemen mocked it as resembling Wu and Chu in their presumptuous assumption of kingship. The continuation of the classics imitated the classics, but gentlemen derided it as a slave or maidservant to the Six Classics. If even these two masters fared thus, how much more those beneath them?

Consider what is recorded in Ban Gu’s Treatise on Literature: thirteen schools for the Book of Changes, nine for the Book of Documents, six for the Book of Odes, thirteen for the rites, twenty-three for the Spring and Autumn Annals, and twelve for the Analects. In all, there were 103 schools associated with the Six Arts. Each developed one aspect and exalted what it favored; some elucidated one another’s work, while others composed writings independently. They were certainly not without brilliance in the literary arena. Yet, though their records multiplied, substantive principle became increasingly obscure; though their efforts at imitation and deliberation were diligent, the standards of the Way did not survive. They did not necessarily illuminate the purport of the Six Classics and the Analects, and compared with the works of Wang Tong and Yang Xiong, they lagged far behind. Why, then, must we enumerate and discuss them all?

As for the writings of Ziyun [Yang Xiong], their heights rise beyond the blue heavens and their depths enter the Yellow Springs. Although he declared that he prized having few who understood him, he could not escape the taunt that his work would serve to cover a sauce jar. Only the writings of Zhongyan [Wang Tong]…

text:
程子謂其極有格言朱子謂其頗近於正
則猶近理者也不但是也自宋玉作對問
以抒志放懷寥廓蓋豪氣之所使也枚乗
賦七發以申規始邪終正蓋七竅之所發
也此則文章流派無預大家分鑣並驅未
攀逸軌者也二子且然況後此者乎自宋
玉既倡而和之者班固之賓戲也東方朔
之客難也揚雄之解嘲也陳琳之應譏也
崔駰之達旨也張衡之應問也蔡邕之釋
===
誨也夏侯湛之抵疑也郤令先之釋譏也
郭景純之客傲也觀其所歸莫不組織玄
黃苞弁今古耿介之意既傷抑鬱之懷靡
懇所謂以文滑稽者也君子何取焉惟達
旨安行慕古人之所序釋誨遺俗以仁義
為淵藪則猶近似者也自枚氏首發而繼
之者傅毅之七激也張衡之七辨也崔駰
之七依也張景陽之七命也曹子建之七
啓也崔瑗之七厲也王粲之七釋也桓麟

translation_en:
…Master Cheng said that it contained many exemplary sayings, and Master Zhu said that it came quite close to what is correct; thus it still approaches true principle. Nor is this all. Song Yu composed Answers to Questions (Dui wen) to express his aspirations, giving his feelings free rein in the boundless expanse: this was surely the impulse of his heroic spirit. Mei Cheng composed the rhapsody Seven Stimuli (Qi fa) to convey admonition, beginning with the deviant and ending with the correct: this surely issued from the seven apertures. These, however, are branches of literary composition that do not rank with the great masters. Taking separate paths and driving abreast, they have yet to attain those lofty tracks. If even these two writers fall short, how much more must their successors?
Once Song Yu had sounded the first note, those who responded included Ban Gu with The Guest’s Jest (Bin xi), Dongfang Shuo with The Guest’s Objections (Ke nan), Yang Xiong with Dispelling Ridicule (Jie chao), Chen Lin with Answering Criticism (Ying ji), Cui Yin with Expressing One’s Intent (Da zhi), Zhang Heng with Answering Questions (Ying wen), Cai Yong with Responding to Admonition (Shi hui), Xiahou Zhan with Countering Doubts (Di yi), Xi Lingxian with Dispelling Criticism (Shi ji), and Guo Jingchun with The Guest’s Taunts (Ke ao). Examining their ultimate purport, one finds that all weave together heaven and earth and encompass past and present [?]. Their spirit of upright independence is already impaired, and their pent-up feelings lack sincerity. This is what is called using writing for verbal sport. What would a gentleman find worthy in it? Only Expressing One’s Intent, with its tranquil conduct and admiration for what the ancients set forth, and Responding to Admonition, with its rejection of vulgar conventions and its adoption of benevolence and righteousness as a refuge, still bear some resemblance to the proper ideal.
After Master Mei first opened the way, those who followed included Fu Yi with Seven Exhortations (Qi ji), Zhang Heng with Seven Discriminations (Qi bian), Cui Yin with Seven Reliances (Qi yi), Zhang Jingyang with Seven Injunctions (Qi ming), Cao Zijian with Seven Disclosures (Qi qi), Cui Yuan with Seven Admonitions (Qi li), Wang Can with Seven Explanations (Qi shi), and Huan Lin…

之七說也左思之七諷也觀其所歸莫不
誇示壞竒鋪張瑰瑋始之以淫侈終之以
居正所謂曲終奏雅者也君子又何取焉
惟七命基德慕皇猷之炳煥七厲叙賢以
儒道爲依歸則猶近似者也然視之六經
論語之旨則猶之韶鄭異音薰蕕殊器判
乎其不合矣嗚呼聖賢不作風雅寖衰若
數子者搴中葉之詞林酌前脩之筆海鳴
宫刻羽遏雲振木猶之陶匏異器並爲入
===
耳之娛黼黻不同俱爲悅目之玩才非不
高也文非不工也然剪綵爲花而貞宰則
泯鎔鑄範物而生理不存昔人謂之虛車
者也區區模倣前人亦何爲哉若杜甫一
編說者謂有三百篇之旨孔明二表人謂
有伊訓說命之風朱晦庵之綱目則有得
夫春秋之意周濂溪之太極圖亦有得夫
大易之旨此則不規規於模擬而自得其
意者也雖然六經未作之前道固未嘗不

之《七說》也，左思之《七諷》也。觀其所歸，莫不誇示壞竒，鋪張瑰瑋，始之以淫侈，終之以居正，所謂曲終奏雅者也。君子又何取焉？惟《七命》基德，慕皇猷之炳煥；《七厲》叙賢，以儒道爲依歸，則猶近似者也。然視之《六經》《論語》之旨，則猶之韶鄭異音，薰蕕殊器，判乎其不合矣。
嗚呼！聖賢不作，風雅寖衰。若數子者，搴中葉之詞林，酌前脩之筆海，鳴宫刻羽，遏雲振木，猶之陶匏異器，並爲入耳之娛；黼黻不同，俱爲悅目之玩。才非不高也，文非不工也，然剪綵爲花而貞宰則泯，鎔鑄範物而生理不存，昔人謂之虛車者也。區區模倣前人，亦何爲哉？若杜甫一編，說者謂有《三百篇》之旨；孔明二表，人謂有《伊訓》《說命》之風；朱晦庵之《綱目》，則有得夫《春秋》之意；周濂溪之《太極圖》，亦有得夫《大易》之旨。此則不規規於模擬而自得其意者也。雖然，《六經》未作之前，道固未嘗不
translation_en:
…his Seven Persuasions, and Zuo Si’s Seven Admonitions. Looking at their ultimate purport, all flaunt bizarre marvels [?] and lavishly elaborate the extraordinary. They begin with excess and extravagance and end by settling upon correctness: what is called “playing an elegant air at the close of the tune.” What, then, should a gentleman find worthy in them? Only Seven Injunctions, which takes virtue as its foundation and admires the brilliance of imperial plans, and Seven Exhortations, which recounts the worthy and takes the Confucian Way as its guiding principle, may still be considered close approximations. Yet, measured against the purport of the Six Classics and the Analects, they are as different as the sounds of Shao music and the music of Zheng, or fragrant and foul-smelling plants kept in separate vessels: plainly incompatible.
Alas! Sages and worthies no longer arise, and the traditions of the Airs and the Odes have gradually declined. These several writers plucked from the forest of letters of the intervening ages and drew from the ocean of their predecessors’ writings. They sounded the gong note and carved out the yu note, arresting the clouds and shaking the trees. Yet, like different instruments of clay and gourd, they merely provide pleasure to the ear; like differing ceremonial embroidery patterns, they are alike objects that delight the eye. Their talent is certainly lofty, and their writing certainly accomplished. Yet they cut colored silk into flowers while effacing the true creative principle; they cast and mold things while leaving no living principle within them. This is what men of old called “empty carriages.” What purpose is served by such petty imitation of predecessors? As for Du Fu’s collected poems, commentators say that they possess the purport of the Three Hundred Poems. Of Kongming’s two memorials, people say that they possess the spirit of the Instructions of Yi and the Charge to Yue. Zhu Hui’an’s Outline and Details grasps something of the meaning of the Spring and Autumn Annals; Zhou Lianxi’s Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate likewise grasps something of the purport of the Great Book of Changes. These writers did not confine themselves to imitation, but apprehended that meaning for themselves. Nevertheless, before the Six Classics were composed, the Way had certainly never been without…

text:
在也學者能以心求經而不以經求經意
傳於肯綮毫釐之中迹異於牝牡驪黃之
外則可以筌蹄章句註脚六經凡言語文
字之學皆可廢也彼漢魏以來諸子著述
之優劣又何足深論哉狂斐之言惟執事
擇焉
第三問
同考試官教諭林批風俗美惡繇乎士習邪正

是策推究時弊卓有定見末以振紀綱脩教化爲言誠探本之論也敬

translation_en:
…existed. If learners can seek the meaning of the Classics through their own minds, rather than seek the Classics through the Classics alone, apprehending their meaning in the minutest essentials while allowing outward expression to differ beyond such superficial distinctions as mare and stallion, black and yellow, then they may treat textual divisions and explanations as fish traps and rabbit snares—means to an end—and regard the Six Classics as footnotes. All learning concerned with words and writing may then be dispensed with. What need, then, to discuss at length the relative merits of the writings of the various masters since the Han and Wei? These are rash and ill-considered words; I leave it to you, Sir, to choose what is worthwhile.

Third Question

Comment by Associate Examiner Lin, Instructor: Whether customs are good or bad depends on whether the habits of scholars are deviant or upright. This policy essay investigates the abuses of the time and displays outstandingly firm judgment. Its concluding call to reinvigorate governing discipline and cultivate moral instruction truly gets to the root of the matter. I respectfully admire it.

Comment by Associate Examiner Chen, District Magistrate: Lofty insight and sound arguments, bearing upon the essentials of governance: the work of one who has long harbored concern for the world.

Comment by Examiner Yan, Right Admonisher: This policy essay on customs answers each point clearly and thoroughly. Moreover, it can pass discerning judgment on the character of men of the Eastern Han and Western Jin, like a suspended mirror reflecting objects without the slightest discrepancy. At the end it again directs attention to moral instruction and governing discipline. This may indeed be called learning with a firm foundation.

Comment by Examiner Kang, Expositor-in-waiting: In conducting themselves in the world, scholars and gentlemen prize remaining unmoved by prevailing customs. This policy essay sets forth the flourishing and decline of customs under the Han and Jin, and the goodness and wickedness of scholars’ habits, as clearly as one sees a blazing fire. The discussion of personal conduct at the end of the essay especially…

title: 嘉靖二十八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
見趨嚮之正是用錄出
習俗之變勢爲之也勢有所必趨故俗有
所必變勢之所趨舉一世之人靡然從之
而不自覺故俗之變也益至於敝而不可
挽時有豪傑者出挺乎自拔於流眾之中
其危操卓識動與道俱好尚審於一時模
範垂於百世夫豈勢之所能局俗之所能
累哉粵自三皇二帝之時風氣龐古天下
大同其政悶悶其民醇醇不知有所謂尚
===
亦不知有所謂俗也世尚之說始於夏而
尚忠迄於商而尚質極於周而尚文夫忠
質文之異尚夏商周之異宜豈故爲是改
革哉抑亦世道之趨者不得不至於此耳
故曰習俗之變勢爲之也然禹貢周官職
方氏辨山川土地所宜皆未始及乎風俗
者豈以盛治之世國不異政家不殊俗本
無美惡之可指邪春秋以降風教漸落民
俗日醨故見於經者則有若十三國風之

punctuated:
見趨嚮之正，是用錄出。

習俗之變，勢爲之也。勢有所必趨，故俗有所必變。勢之所趨，舉一世之人靡然從之而不自覺，故俗之變也，益至於敝而不可挽。時有豪傑者出，挺乎自拔於流眾之中，其危操卓識，動與道俱，好尚審於一時，模範垂於百世，夫豈勢之所能局、俗之所能累哉！粵自三皇二帝之時，風氣龐古，天下大同，其政悶悶，其民醇醇，不知有所謂尚，亦不知有所謂俗也。世尚之說，始於夏而尚忠，迄於商而尚質，極於周而尚文。夫忠質文之異尚，夏商周之異宜，豈故爲是改革哉？抑亦世道之趨者，不得不至於此耳。故曰：「習俗之變，勢爲之也。」然《禹貢》《周官》職方氏辨山川土地所宜，皆未始及乎風俗者，豈以盛治之世，國不異政，家不殊俗，本無美惡之可指邪？春秋以降，風教漸落，民俗日醨，故見於經者，則有若十三國風之
translation_en:
…reveals the uprightness of his aims; for this reason, it has been selected for inclusion.

Changes in customary practices are brought about by the force of circumstances. Since circumstances necessarily tend in certain directions, customs necessarily undergo certain changes. Wherever circumstances lead, the people of an entire age follow in submission, without themselves realizing it. Thus, as customs change, they grow increasingly corrupt, until the process cannot be reversed. At times, an outstanding man emerges, resolutely raising himself above the common throng. With lofty integrity and exceptional discernment, his every action accords with the Way. His preferences are soundly judged in his own age, and his example is handed down through a hundred generations. How could such a man be confined by circumstances or encumbered by custom!

From the time of the Three Sovereigns and Two Emperors, the prevailing ethos was simple and ancient, and all under Heaven enjoyed great harmony. Government was unobtrusive, and the people were pure and sincere. They knew neither what were called prevailing preferences nor what were called customs. Accounts of the preferences of successive ages begin with the Xia, which prized loyalty, continue with the Shang, which prized simplicity, and culminate in the Zhou, which prized refinement. These differing preferences for loyalty, simplicity, and refinement suited the differing needs of the Xia, Shang, and Zhou. Were these changes deliberately contrived? Rather, the tendencies of the age made it inevitable that things should come to this. Thus I say: “Changes in customary practices are brought about by the force of circumstances.”

Yet the Tribute of Yu (Yu gong) and the account of the Director of the Bureau of Relations (Zhifang shi) in the Offices of Zhou (Zhou guan), while distinguishing mountains, rivers, lands, and what each was suited to, never touched upon customs. Was this because, in an age of flourishing government, states did not differ in their administration, nor households in their customs, so that there were no good or bad customs to point out? From the Spring and Autumn period onward, moral influence and instruction gradually declined, and popular customs grew daily less substantial. Thus, among the accounts found in the Classics, there are, for example, those in the Airs of the Thirteen States…

title: 嘉靖二十八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
詩載之為甚悉見於史者則有若班固地
理之志紀之為最詳亦以風聲氣習與世
污隆故經史兼而收之以徵夫世道之變
耳時至東漢光武明章率興教化風厲儒
術一時之士雅尚清議以節義自勵者斯
彬彬然顯焉觀張綱埋輪都亭而貴戚為
之屏氣杜喬立朝正色而善類為之傾心
破柱戮姦不畏權宦李膺之行何偉也登
車攬轡誓志澄清范滂之望何重也之數
===
公者立身之大義許國之奇忠皆卓乎不
可尚矣其有不盡然者則暮夜投金若王
密恭遜媚時若胡廣崔烈之入錢冒爵自
貽銅臭之譏荀彧之委心事瞞甘蹈失身
之戾回視四公蓋不啻天淵之弗相及矣
夫豈清議之所能倡邪迨及西晉武帝惠
懷彝章紊廢政教陵夷一時之士競尚清
談以禮法自棄者蓋比比然見焉觀王戎
之與世浮沉而無所匡救何晏之糟粕經

詩，載之為甚悉；見於史者，則有若班固地理之志，紀之為最詳。亦以風聲氣習與世污隆，故經史兼而收之，以徵夫世道之變耳。
時至東漢，光武、明、章率興教化，風厲儒術。一時之士，雅尚清議，以節義自勵者，斯彬彬然顯焉。觀張綱埋輪都亭，而貴戚為之屏氣；杜喬立朝正色，而善類為之傾心；破柱戮姦，不畏權宦，李膺之行何偉也；登車攬轡，誓志澄清，范滂之望何重也！之數公者，立身之大義，許國之奇忠，皆卓乎不可尚矣。其有不盡然者，則暮夜投金若王密，恭遜媚時若胡廣，崔烈之入錢冒爵，自貽銅臭之譏；荀彧之委心事瞞，甘蹈失身之戾。回視四公，蓋不啻天淵之弗相及矣，夫豈清議之所能倡邪？
迨及西晉武帝、惠、懷，彝章紊廢，政教陵夷。一時之士，競尚清談，以禮法自棄者，蓋比比然見焉。觀王戎之與世浮沉，而無所匡救；何晏之糟粕經
translation_en:
…poems, which record these matters in great detail. Among historical writings, Ban Gu’s Treatise on Geography records them most fully. Since prevailing influences and customary habits rise and decline along with the age, both the classics and the histories include them as evidence of changes in the moral condition of the times.
When the Eastern Han arrived, Emperors Guangwu, Ming, and Zhang all promoted moral instruction and encouraged Confucian learning. Among the scholars of that age, those who prized upright public judgment and spurred themselves on through integrity and righteousness emerged in cultivated distinction. Consider Zhang Gang, who buried his carriage wheels at the capital’s pavilion, making powerful imperial relatives hold their breath in fear; Du Qiao, who stood at court with a stern countenance, winning the wholehearted allegiance of worthy men; and Li Ying, who broke open a pillar to execute a villain, undaunted by powerful eunuchs—how magnificent his conduct! Fan Pang mounted his carriage, took up the reins, and pledged himself to cleanse the realm—how weighty his reputation! These gentlemen were all unsurpassably eminent in the great righteousness by which they conducted themselves and the extraordinary loyalty with which they committed themselves to the state. Yet there were exceptions: Wang Mi offered gold in the dead of night; Hu Guang courted the favor of his contemporaries through deferential compliance; Cui Lie paid money to obtain rank, bringing upon himself the taunt of the “stench of copper”; and Xun Yu devoted himself to serving Man [Cao Cao], willingly incurring the guilt of compromising his integrity. Compared with the four gentlemen, they were separated by more than the gulf between heaven and the depths. How could upright public judgment have encouraged such conduct?
By the reigns of Emperors Wu, Hui, and Huai of the Western Jin, established institutions had fallen into disorder and disuse, and government and moral instruction had declined. Scholars of the age competed in prizing pure conversation, and those who abandoned ritual propriety and standards of conduct appeared everywhere. Consider Wang Rong, who drifted with the world without doing anything to correct or rescue it; and He Yan, who treated the classics as dregs…

title: 嘉靖二十八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
藉而竟成風流居喪飲酒無異平日阮籍
之汚行可鄙也鹿車放逸壺鍤自隨劉伶
之失德可議也之數人者非毀先王之道
藝破壞聖人之藩墻皆藐乎不足齒矣亦
有不盡然者則渡江擊楫如祖逖灑淚新
亭如王導劉琨之聞雞起舞期定乎中原
陶侃之運甓習勞志存乎王室回視四子
蓋不啻薰蕕之弗相近矣夫豈清談之所
能累邪夫俗之有推遷者勢也趨之有邪
===
正者人也趨之正則俗雖惡不能誘而移
矣趨之邪則俗雖善不能化而入矣故東
漢之崇節義謂成於清議可也謂全藉於
清議不可也西晉之廢禮法謂溺於清談
可也謂不由於清談不可也是故俗也者
一人倡之千人和之一日行之百年效之
其始也倏然而從其既也恬然而習其終
也帖然而安非有豪傑者出則習與智長
化與心成不隨之而變者幾希孟軻氏曰

===
正者人也趨之正則俗雖惡不能誘而移
矣趨之邪則俗雖善不能化而入矣故東
漢之崇節義謂成於清議可也謂全籍於
清議不可也西晉之廢禮法謂溺於清談
可也謂不由於清談不可也是故俗也者
一人倡之千人和之一日行之百年效之
其始也倏然而從其既也恬然而習其終
也帖然而安非有豪傑者出則習與智長
化與心成不隨之而變者幾希孟軻氏曰
punctuated:
藉而竟成風流；居喪飲酒，無異平日，阮籍之汚行可鄙也；鹿車放逸，壺鍤自隨，劉伶之失德可議也。之數人者，非毀先王之道藝，破壞聖人之藩墻，皆藐乎不足齒矣。亦有不盡然者，則渡江擊楫如祖逖，灑淚新亭如王導，劉琨之聞雞起舞，期定乎中原，陶侃之運甓習勞，志存乎王室。回視四子，蓋不啻薰蕕之弗相近矣。夫豈清談之所能累邪？
夫俗之有推遷者，勢也；趨之有邪正者，人也。趨之正，則俗雖惡，不能誘而移矣；趨之邪，則俗雖善，不能化而入矣。故東漢之崇節義，謂成於清議可也，謂全藉於清議不可也；西晉之廢禮法，謂溺於清談可也，謂不由於清談不可也。是故俗也者，一人倡之，千人和之；一日行之，百年效之。其始也，倏然而從；其既也，恬然而習；其終也，帖然而安。非有豪傑者出，則習與智長，化與心成，不隨之而變者幾希。孟軻氏曰：
translation_en:
…reducing the classics to dregs, yet ultimately setting a fashionable example. Drinking wine during mourning, just as on ordinary days: Ruan Ji’s foul conduct deserves contempt. Roaming unrestrained in a small cart, with a wine jar and spade accompanying him: Liu Ling’s failure of virtue deserves censure. These several men [?] disparaged the Way and arts of the former kings and broke down the protective walls of the sages; all were contemptible and unworthy of mention. Yet there were exceptions: Zu Ti struck his oar while crossing the river; Wang Dao shed tears at Xinting; Liu Kun rose to practice swordsmanship upon hearing the cock crow, aspiring to pacify the Central Plain; and Tao Kan carried bricks to accustom himself to toil, his ambitions devoted to the imperial house. Looking back at the four men mentioned earlier, the difference was no less than that between fragrant and foul-smelling herbs. How could pure conversation have implicated such men?
That customs shift with time is a matter of prevailing circumstances; whether one’s course is deviant or upright depends on the individual. If one’s course is upright, even bad customs cannot entice one to change. If one’s course is deviant, even good customs cannot transform one and bring one within their influence. Thus, concerning the Eastern Han’s esteem for integrity and righteousness, one may say that it was fostered by public moral criticism, but not that it depended entirely upon such criticism. Concerning the Western Jin’s abandonment of ritual and law, one may say that it sank into pure conversation; one cannot say that this did not result from pure conversation. Customs, then, are something one person initiates and a thousand echo, something practiced for a single day and imitated for a hundred years. At first, people suddenly follow; thereafter, they placidly grow accustomed to it; finally, they settle comfortably into it. Unless outstanding men arise, habits grow alongside understanding, and the effects of habituation take shape together with the mind; few indeed avoid changing along with them. Meng Ke said: …

title: 嘉靖二十八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
待文王而興者凡民也若夫豪傑之士雖
無文王猶興何者蓋豪傑之士其所趨者
正也且豪傑之與庸人其初豈甚相遠哉
特以所趨有邪正故其所就有高下寓于
波流風靡之中而有確乎不拔之操非豪
傑能然哉嗚呼大公至正之道不行於世
久矣士而崇節義無可議者其流而為清
談則祖尚虛無遺落世事猶無甚害也習
俗之壞莫大於士務詭而亂道士務詭而
===
亂道則義利不明毁譽失真是非交溷目
巧詐為通明説廉靖為矯激稱容姦為大
體指剛方為亡情以持禄保位為賢以竭
忠盡節為愚以奔競進取為能以恬退自
守為拙謂刻薄辦事為有才謂重厚長者
為無用蒸淫日久而不自覺則其勢猶水
之趨壑也其始若無所患而其末也奔馳
潰決障塞無所施其力矣是可不寒心乎
惟在識其勢以亟反之耳若夫矯偏釐陋

punctuated:
「待文王而興者，凡民也；若夫豪傑之士，雖無文王猶興。」何者？蓋豪傑之士，其所趨者正也。且豪傑之與庸人，其初豈甚相遠哉？特以所趨有邪正，故其所就有高下。寓于波流風靡之中，而有確乎不拔之操，非豪傑能然哉？

嗚呼！大公至正之道不行於世久矣。士而崇節義，無可議者；其流而為清談，則祖尚虛無，遺落世事，猶無甚害也。習俗之壞，莫大於士務詭而亂道。士務詭而亂道，則義利不明，毁譽失真，是非交溷。目巧詐為通明，説廉靖為矯激，稱容姦為大體，指剛方為亡情；以持禄保位為賢，以竭忠盡節為愚，以奔競進取為能，以恬退自守為拙；謂刻薄辦事為有才，謂重厚長者為無用。蒸淫日久而不自覺，則其勢猶水之趨壑也。其始若無所患，而其末也，奔馳潰決，障塞無所施其力矣。是可不寒心乎？惟在識其勢以亟反之耳。若夫矯偏釐陋
translation_en:
“Those who await King Wen before they are stirred to action are ordinary people. As for outstanding men, even without King Wen they are still stirred to action.” Why is this? Because what outstanding men pursue is right. Moreover, were outstanding men and ordinary people so very different at the outset? It is simply that their pursuits are either deviant or upright, and thus their attainments are either low or high. To dwell amid currents that sweep people along and winds that bend them, yet maintain a resolve firm and unshakable—could anyone but an outstanding man do this?

Alas! The way of utmost impartiality and rectitude has long gone unpracticed in the world. When scholars esteem integrity and righteousness, there is nothing to criticize. Even when this tendency degenerates into “pure conversation,” so that they revere emptiness and nonbeing and neglect worldly affairs, the harm is still not very great. Nothing corrupts customs more gravely than scholars pursuing deceit and throwing the Way into disorder. When scholars pursue deceit and throw the Way into disorder, righteousness and profit cease to be clearly distinguished, blame and praise lose their truth, and right and wrong become confused. Cunning deception is regarded as perceptiveness; incorruptibility and quiet restraint are called affected extremism; tolerating wickedness is praised as attending to the larger concerns; firmness and rectitude are condemned as heartlessness. Holding on to stipends and securing one’s position count as worthiness, while giving one’s utmost loyalty and fulfilling one’s integrity count as folly. Scrambling competitively for advancement counts as ability, while quietly withdrawing and keeping one’s principles count as ineptitude. Those who conduct affairs with harshness are called talented, while substantial and generous elders are called useless. When this influence has permeated society for a long time without people becoming aware of it, its momentum is like water rushing into a ravine. At first there seems nothing to fear, but in the end it races onward and bursts its banks, and barriers and embankments can no longer exert any effect. Can this fail to chill the heart? All depends on recognizing this momentum and urgently reversing it. As for correcting deviations and remedying debased practices…

title: 嘉靖二十八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
之術豈必體堯蹈舜然後乃理哉詩曰爾
之教矣民胥效矣言教化之不可不敦也
又曰勉勉我王綱紀四方言紀綱之不可
不振也蓋紀綱者整飭天下之大務教化
者轉移天下之大機紀綱不振則習棼而
渙政舛而違而無以致治教化不敦則趨
繆而欹事逸而縱而無以成道是故握風
俗之樞者有教化以淑人心又有紀綱以
齊民行則天下之俗有不翕然而易者吾
===
不信矣一得之愚敢僭述以為明問復惟
進而裁之
第四問
同考試官教諭馮 批 理財乃經國大務而法莫善
於成周此篇酌古準今敷答無遺區處尤當末復以節儉為言其識治體者乎
同考試官教諭張 批 理財之策塲中作者率多
掇拾陳言汎濫不切是篇論成周所以得及後世所以失井井有條且
區畫時事卓有定見結末數言尤探本之論錄之

punctuated:
之術，豈必體堯蹈舜，然後乃理哉？《詩》曰：「爾之教矣，民胥效矣。」言教化之不可不敦也。又曰：「勉勉我王，綱紀四方。」言紀綱之不可不振也。蓋紀綱者，整飭天下之大務；教化者，轉移天下之大機。紀綱不振，則習棼而渙，政舛而違，而無以致治；教化不敦，則趨繆而欹，事逸而縱，而無以成道。是故握風俗之樞者，有教化以淑人心，又有紀綱以齊民行，則天下之俗有不翕然而易者，吾不信矣。一得之愚，敢僭述以為明問復，惟進而裁之。

第四問

同考試官教諭馮批：「理財乃經國大務，而法莫善於成周。此篇酌古準今，敷答無遺，區處尤當。末復以節儉為言，其識治體者乎！」

同考試官教諭張批：「理財之策，塲中作者率多掇拾陳言，汎濫不切。是篇論成周所以得及後世所以失，井井有條，且區畫時事，卓有定見。結末數言，尤探本之論，錄之。」
translation_en:
…as for the means of correcting these deviations and remedying these abuses, must one necessarily embody Yao and follow Shun before order can be achieved? The Book of Odes says: “Your teaching—all the people emulate it.” This means that moral instruction must be strengthened. It also says: “Diligent is our king, ordering the four quarters.” This means that governing discipline must be invigorated. Governing discipline is the great undertaking by which the realm is brought into order; moral instruction is the crucial means by which the realm is transformed. If governing discipline is not invigorated, customary practices become tangled and lax, and administration goes awry and becomes inconsistent, leaving no means of achieving good government. If moral instruction is not strengthened, people’s inclinations become misguided and crooked, and affairs are handled carelessly and without restraint, leaving no means of bringing the Way to fulfillment. Thus, when those who control the pivotal means of shaping customs employ moral instruction to improve people’s hearts, together with governing discipline to regulate their conduct, I cannot believe that any customs in the realm will fail to change in concert. I venture presumptuously to set forth this single insight of mine, foolish though it may be, in reply to your enlightened question. I respectfully submit it for your judgment.

Fourth Question

Associate Examiner Feng, Instructor, comments: “Managing finances is a major undertaking in governing the state, and no methods surpass those of the Zhou at its height. This essay weighs ancient practice against present circumstances and answers fully, omitting nothing; its arrangements are especially appropriate. At the end it again speaks of frugality. Surely its author understands the essentials of government!”

Associate Examiner Zhang, Instructor, comments: “Among the candidates writing policy essays on financial management in the examination hall, most merely gather up stale sayings, rambling without addressing the issue. This essay explains in clear order why the Zhou at its height succeeded and why later ages failed. Moreover, in proposing arrangements for contemporary affairs, it displays remarkably firm judgment. Its closing remarks especially probe the root of the matter. Select it for inclusion.”

title: 嘉靖二十八年順天府鄉試錄
text:
同考試官進士李批理財一事方今急務子能
詳悉古今失得而惓惓於節用是有經國之慮者宜錄以式
考試官右贊善閻批叅論古今理財得失若指諸
掌中間區畫數事皆鑿鑿可行有學有用之士也
考試官侍講康批理財人能言之是作考論古
今盈縮之故而裁以獨見且通達
國體諳練時務豈韋布而有天下之慮者耶
愚聞之天下之財其豐也固必有其源而
其耗也亦必有其由弗開其源則無根之
===
木不能至拱把無源之水不能達江河非
務本之論也弗去其耗則山林不能供野
火江海不能實漏卮非救時之策也故必
力本而導利有以開財之源酌盈以濟虛
有以節財之流則不必規規於理財而財
自充國自富矣請因明問而復之易曰何
以守位曰仁何以聚人曰財言足國裕民
惟財爲急也書曰水火金木土穀惟修正
德利用厚生惟和言阜財養民惟政爲先

考試官右賛善闞　批〔叅論古今理財得失若指諸掌中間區畫數事皆鑿鑿可行有學有用之士也〕

愚聞之天下之財其豐也固必有其源而
其耗也亦必有其由弗開其源則無根之
